explanation:
2nd true. $\frac{d}{dx}\max(0,x) = 1$ for every $x > 0$ — exactly $1$, not approximately, which is the whole appeal against sigmoid and tanh.

1st false. The range is $[0,\infty)$, so the mean activation is positive. Not zero-centred; that is one of the standing criticisms.

4th false, and this is the trap. ReLU removes vanishing gradients only in the positive domain. For $x < 0$ the gradient is exactly $0$ — not small, zero.

3rd true, and it is the same fact as the 4th. A neuron whose pre-activation is negative for every input in the dataset receives zero gradient forever and can never recover. That is the dying ReLU problem, and it is why leaky ReLU exists.

explanation:
Only one option is correct, and the 2nd is why. Weight sharing produces translation equivariance, not invariance: shift the input and the feature map shifts with it — the response moves, it does not stay put. Invariance would mean the output does not change at all, which is what a global pooling layer on top provides, not the convolution itself. One word, and it is the difference between the two most confused terms in the course (Q23, Q59).

The 1st is the other one worth thinking about. Weight sharing does not reduce FLOPs. The same dot product is still computed at every spatial location — what shrinks is the number of distinct weights you must store and learn. It is local connectivity (a small kernel rather than a dense layer) that reduces FLOPs; the two properties are usually introduced together and are constantly conflated.

3rd false. Because the kernel is applied position by position, a convolutional layer is defined for an input of any spatial size. That is precisely what makes fully convolutional networks possible — and it is the same fact that Q51 and ScanComplete depend on.

explanation:
Why saddles dominate. At a critical point in $d$ dimensions the Hessian has $d$ eigenvalues. A local minimum needs all of them positive. If signs were independent and equally likely, that is one outcome in $2^d$ — so for any realistic $d$ almost every critical point has at least one negative direction, i.e. is a saddle.

Why the 3rd is backwards. At a saddle the true gradient is zero, so full-batch gradient descent has nothing to move it and stalls. SGD's mini-batch gradient is almost never exactly zero, and that noise knocks it off the saddle. Noise is the escape mechanism, so the method with more noise escapes more easily.

Why the 4th matters in practice. You rarely land exactly on a critical point. What actually costs you is the large, nearly flat region around it, where the gradient is tiny but non-zero and progress crawls for many epochs.

Why a saddle needs two dimensions. On the left, a one-parameter loss has only two kinds of critical point: the curve turns up or it turns down. On the right, the red point is a minimum along $\theta_1$ and a maximum along $\theta_2$ — the gradient is zero, yet an escape route exists. Full-batch gradient descent cannot find it, because the thing it follows is exactly zero; SGD's noise pushes it off the ridge and down the amber direction. In $d$ dimensions there are $d$ such signs to get right, which is why genuine minima are rare and saddles are everywhere.
stem: In high-dimensional deep learning loss landscapes:
options: saddle points are far more common than local minima
at a local minimum all Hessian eigenvalues are positive
full-batch gradient descent escapes saddle points more easily than SGD
plateaus around saddle points slow training even when not exactly at the critical point

explanation:
Every option is true here — check rather than assume, and note that the scaling is by $\sqrt{d_k}$ and not by $d_k$, which is the form Q6 asks you to justify.

2nd true, and it is the reason positional encodings exist. Permute the input tokens and the set of attention outputs permutes identically; nothing in $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d_k})V$ refers to position. Order has to be injected into the embeddings before the first layer or the model is blind to it.

3rd true. A hard lookup “fetch item $i$” is not differentiable in $i$. The softmax replaces it with a weighted average over all items, which is differentiable everywhere — soft indexing is what makes attention trainable at all.

4th true. $QK^{\top}$ requires $Q$ and $K$ to share their last dimension. Only $V$ is free to differ, with dimension $d_v$.

explanation:
Take $q$ and $k$ with independent components of mean $0$ and variance $1$. Then \[ q\cdot k = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(q\cdot k) = d_k, \qquad \text{typical magnitude} = \sqrt{d_k}. \] The quantity that grows with dimension is the standard deviation, and it grows as $\sqrt{d_k}$, not $d_k$. Dividing by the standard deviation is what restores a constant scale whatever $d_k$ is.

Dividing by $d_k$ would over-correct, shrinking the scores towards zero and flattening the softmax into a near-uniform distribution — the opposite failure, and just as useless.

Both distributions sum to one — the softmax normalises either way, so the total bar height is identical. What changes is the sharpness. On the left the scores are large enough that the softmax saturates: one weight goes to $1$, the rest to $0$, and in that regime the softmax's gradient is essentially zero, so no learning signal flows back through the attention weights. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ keeps the scores near $\pm 1$ whatever the head dimension, which is where the softmax stays soft.

options: because the softmax is invariant to scaling by $d_k$
because $\sqrt{d_k}$ is cheaper to compute
because the variance of the dot product grows as $d_k$, so its standard deviation grows as $\sqrt{d_k}$
because dividing by $d_k$ would make the attention weights negative

explanation:
Compare the two per-layer costs directly: \[ \underbrace{O(n^2 d)}_{\text{self-attention}} \;\;\text{vs}\;\; \underbrace{O(n d^2)}_{\text{recurrent}} . \] Divide both by $nd$: the comparison is simply $n$ against $d$. Self-attention wins when $n < d$.

This is why the trade-off is real rather than academic. With $d_{\text{model}} = 512$ and a sentence of 30 tokens, $n \ll d$ and attention is cheap. With a high-resolution image flattened to thousands of patches, $n \gg d$ and the quadratic term dominates — which is the entire motivation for Swin's windows (Q33, Q44, Q57) and for the Sparse Transformer (Q40).

“Submanifold” is a statement about the output. SSC computes an output only where a site is already active, so the active set comes out of the layer exactly as it went in.

Why the other three fail the test. Regular SC writes an output wherever the kernel touches an active site, so the active set grows by one ring per layer — that is the dilation problem (Q34, Q51). Strided SC changes the grid itself. Sparse up-convolution deliberately creates new active sites. Only SSC leaves the set alone.

The T-Net is the classic trap. It predicts a transformation matrix that aligns the cloud spatially — that is spatial invariance, a different property entirely. explanation:
1st and 2nd together are the definition, and the pair is easy to garble. SSC writes only at already-active locations, but it still reads from inactive neighbours and treats them as zero. Reading is harmless; it is writing to new locations that causes the trouble.

3rd true — that is exactly what SSC was invented for. Because the active set is preserved, it cannot grow layer by layer, so the dilation of Q18 does not happen.

4th true, and it restates the 1st as a property of the whole layer. The output is active exactly where the input was, so the sparsity pattern passes through unchanged — which is what makes a stack of SSC layers affordable.

And it is also the limitation, seen from the other side. Preserving the active set is precisely what stops two components that are not already touching from ever communicating: no output is written in the gap between them, so information can never cross it. That is why real networks interleave striding, pooling or occasional regular SC layers. The fix and the limitation are one fact, not two. Q51 and Q58 work this through with a picture.

explanation:
A layer is anisotropic when the weight given to a neighbour depends on what that neighbour is, not merely on where it sits in the graph. Attention coefficients, edge-conditioned messages and relation-specific weights all read features or edge types, so all three qualify.

Degree normalisation does not. $1/\sqrt{\tilde D_{ii}\tilde D_{jj}}$ depends on both endpoints, which makes it look anisotropic — but only through fixed structure, never through content. Change the node features and the coefficient is unchanged. GCN is isotropic, and this is the cleanest way to see why GAT is a genuine step beyond it rather than a re-weighting.

explanation:
$\mathcal{D}^2 = (x_i - x_j)^{\top} M (x_i - x_j)$ is only a valid squared distance if it is never negative, i.e. if $M$ is positive semi-definite. Optimising $M$ directly would mean projecting back onto the PSD cone after every step — an awkward constrained problem.

Writing $M = W^{\top}W$ makes the constraint structural: for any real $W$ whatsoever, $z^{\top}W^{\top}Wz = \lVert Wz \rVert^2 \ge 0$ automatically. So $W$ can be optimised freely by ordinary gradient descent and the constraint can never be violated.

It is the constraint, not the cost, that is the reason — and note the reading this gives: learning a Mahalanobis distance is the same thing as learning a linear embedding $W$ and using plain Euclidean distance in it.

explanation:
Softmax training optimises for one thing: getting the argmax right. That makes classes separable — and separable by angle, since the logit is $w_c^{\top}z$ — but it stops caring the instant a sample is on the correct side of the boundary.

So it gives you no reason for a class to be compact (samples may sprawl along their wedge), no gap between neighbouring classes (the boundary can be touched from both sides), and therefore no threshold that works: the distance between two same-class samples at opposite ends of a wedge can easily exceed the distance between two different-class samples that sit either side of a boundary.

That last consequence is the one that matters for similarity learning, because retrieval and verification both need exactly that threshold. It is what angular-margin losses such as ArcFace are built to supply, by inserting the margin into the angle of the true class only.

Both pictures classify perfectly. Every point on the left is on the correct side of every boundary, so the softmax loss is happy and has no gradient left to give. But pick a distance threshold: on the left, the blue point near the centre is closer to the green points than to the blue point at the rim, so no threshold separates same-class from different-class pairs. On the right the classes are compact and separated by a deliberate margin, so a single threshold works — which is what verification and retrieval actually need. Classification and similarity are different objectives, and only the second one asks for this picture.

explanation:
Filled in: A dilated convolution has effective kernel size $K_{\text{eff}} = \mathbf{D(K-1)+1}$. The receptive-field recurrence is $R_l = \mathbf{R_{l-1} + (K_{\text{eff},l}-1)\,J_{l-1}}$, and the jump recurrence is $J_l = \mathbf{J_{l-1}\,S_l}$. Read each one. $K_{\text{eff}}$: a dilated kernel has $K$ taps with $D-1$ gaps between them, so it spans $D(K-1)+1$ positions — $D = 1$ recovers $K_{\text{eff}} = K$. $J_l$: the jump is how far apart, in input pixels, two adjacent units of layer $l$ are; it is the running product of all strides so far. $R_l$: adding a layer widens the field by $K_{\text{eff}}-1$ steps, and each step is worth $J_{l-1}$ input pixels — the jump of the layer below, not the current one. Getting that index wrong is the commonest error, and Q42 is where it shows.

Start the recursion at $R_0 = 1$, $J_0 = 1$. Padding never appears — it moves where outputs sit, not how far back they reach.

Filled in: Self-attention has complexity $O(n^2 d)$ per layer, $O(1)$ sequential operations, and maximum path length $O(1)$. A recurrent layer has $O(n d^2)$, $O(n)$ and $O(n)$ respectively. Side by side, which is how it is worth memorising:

complexity / layersequential opsmax path length
self-attention$O(n^2 d)$$O(1)$$O(1)$
recurrent$O(n d^2)$$O(n)$$O(n)$

The middle column is the one that changed the field: an RNN must perform $n$ steps in order, so it cannot be parallelised along the sequence, while attention does everything at once. The third column is why long-range dependencies became learnable — in an RNN the signal between two distant tokens passes through $O(n)$ multiplications and vanishes; in attention they are one hop apart. The price is the first column, which is quadratic and is what Q8 and Q11 quantify.

explanation:
Filled in: The unnormalised graph Laplacian is $L = \mathbf{D - A}$ and the normalised one is $L_N = \mathbf{D^{-1/2} L D^{-1/2} = I - D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}}$. The GCN propagation rule is $H^{(l+1)} = \mathbf{\sigma\!\left(\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A \tilde D^{-1/2} H^{(l)} W^{(l)}\right)}$. Note the tildes, because this is where marks and real implementations are lost. $\tilde A = A + I$ adds the self-loop first, and $\tilde D$ is the degree matrix of $\tilde A$, not of $A$. Computing $\tilde D$ from $A$ and then using it with $\tilde A$ is a common and silent bug — every node's own contribution is then mis-weighted.

Why the self-loop is needed at all. Without $+I$, the propagation replaces each node's features entirely by its neighbours' and discards its own, so a node cannot remember anything about itself.

Filled in: A distance satisfying every metric axiom except identity of indiscernibles is a pseudo-metric. Training only on hard negatives risks network collapse, because a constant encoder pays exactly $m$ (the margin) per triplet. Identity of indiscernibles is the axiom $\mathcal{D}(x,y) = 0 \Rightarrow x = y$. Drop it and you permit $\mathcal{D}(x,y) = 0$ for genuinely different $x$ and $y$ — which is exactly what a collapsed encoder produces, mapping everything to one point.

So the two blanks are the same failure seen from two directions, and the third blank explains why gradient descent finds it. With the triplet loss $\max(0,\ \mathcal{D}(a,p) - \mathcal{D}(a,n) + m)$, a constant encoder makes both distances $0$ and the loss exactly $m$ on every triplet — a flat, finite, easily reached plateau. Feed the network only its hardest negatives and that plateau can be a better deal than solving the actual problem. See Q53.

explanation: Two of these are commonly got the wrong way round. Flattening must precede the projection, because the projection is a matrix acting on a vector. And the [class] token is prepended after positional embeddings are added to the patch tokens — it is not a patch and does not get a patch position.

A transformer is a GNN on a complete graph — that identification is worth carrying, because it explains both why attention is expressive and why it costs $O(n^2)$ while a sparse GNN costs $O(|\mathcal{E}|)$. Q59 draws it.

The four differ in where the split between space and time happens:

spatio-temporalcno split at all — attention over every space-time token at once. Most expressive, quadratic in $n_t n_h n_w$

explanation:
Answer: $\mathbf{19}$

Run the recurrence from Q31 with $R_0 = 1$, $J_0 = 1$:

layer$K_{\text{eff}}$$R$$J$ after
——$R_0 = 1$$J_0 = 1$
L1 ($K{=}5,S{=}1,D{=}1$)$5$$1 + 4\cdot 1 = 5$$1$
L2 ($K{=}3,S{=}2,D{=}1$)$3$$5 + 2\cdot 1 = 7$$2$
L3 ($K{=}3,S{=}1,D{=}3$)$3(3{-}1){+}1 = 7$$7 + 6\cdot 2 = \mathbf{19}$$2$

Check it by hand, because trusting the recurrence blindly is how the mistake survives. Number the input $0,1,2,\dots$ One L3 output reads three L2 units spaced $D = 3$ apart: L2 units $0, 3, 6$. Each L2 unit $u$ reads L1 units $2u, 2u{+}1, 2u{+}2$ (stride 2, $K = 3$), giving $\{0,1,2\}$, $\{6,7,8\}$, $\{12,13,14\}$. Each L1 unit $v$ reads inputs $v \dots v{+}4$. Lowest input touched: $0$. Highest: $14 + 4 = 18$. So the field spans inputs $0$ through $18$ — $\mathbf{19}$ positions.

Three ways to get it wrong. Using $J_l$ instead of $J_{l-1}$ in the update; forgetting that dilation inflates $K$ before it enters the formula; and letting padding into the calculation, which never belongs there.
stem: A 1D network has: L1 convolution ($K=5$, $S=1$, $P=2$, $D=1$); L2 convolution ($K=3$, $S=2$, $P=1$, $D=1$); L3 dilated convolution ($K=3$, $S=1$, $P=2$, $D=3$). What is the receptive field of one output neuron of L3?

explanation:
Answer: $d_k = \mathbf{64}$; $W^{O}$ has $\mathbf{262{,}144}$ parameters

$d_k = d_{\text{model}}/h = 512/8 = 64$. The heads partition the width rather than adding to it, which is why multi-head attention costs essentially the same as single-head over the full 512 — every term in the FLOP count contains $h$ only through $h \cdot d_k$ or $h \cdot d_v$, both equal to $d_{\text{model}}$, so $h$ cancels.

$W^{O} \in \mathbb{R}^{h d_v \times d_{\text{model}}} = \mathbb{R}^{512 \times 512}$, so $512^2 = \mathbf{262{,}144}$ parameters. Its job is to mix the concatenated heads, which are otherwise independent — without it, the head outputs would simply sit side by side in the vector and never interact.
stem: A transformer layer has $d_{\text{model}} = 512$ and $h = 8$ heads. What is $d_k$? How many parameters does the output projection $W^{O}$ contain, ignoring biases?

explanation:
Answer: $\mathbf{128 \times 128 \times 192}$

Three steps, in order:

  1. Patch partition. $1024/4 = 256$, so Stage 1 operates on a $256 \times 256$ grid with $C = 96$ channels.
  2. Patch merging concatenates each $2\times2$ neighbourhood: spatial dimensions halve to $128 \times 128$, channels quadruple to $4C = 384$.
  3. Linear projection halves that to $2C = 192$.

Result: $\mathbf{128 \times 128 \times 192}$.

The pattern to remember is $2C$ per stage, not $4C$. Merging alone would quadruple the channels; the projection immediately halves it, so each stage doubles the width while quartering the spatial extent — which is the classic CNN pyramid shape, and exactly the hierarchy plain ViT lacks.
stem: A Swin backbone receives a $1024\times1024$ RGB image with patch size $P = 4$ and base channel dimension $C = 96$. What tensor shape enters Stage 2, i.e. after one patch-merging step, which halves the concatenated channel dimension?

explanation:
Answer: $\mathbf{64{,}480}$

The formula is $K_d K_h K_w \cdot C_{\text{in}} \cdot C_{\text{out}} + C_{\text{out}}$, one bias per output channel. \[\begin{aligned} \text{layer 1:} \quad & \underbrace{3\cdot3\cdot3}_{27}\cdot 1 \cdot 16 + 16 = 432 + 16 = \mathbf{448} \\ \text{layer 2:} \quad & \underbrace{5\cdot5\cdot5}_{125}\cdot 16 \cdot 32 + 32 = 64{,}000 + 32 = \mathbf{64{,}032} \end{aligned}\] Total $448 + 64{,}032 = \mathbf{64{,}480}$.

Three ways to lose the mark. Forgetting the biases gives $64{,}432$. Using $3\times3$ and $5\times5$ instead of the 3D kernels gives a number roughly a third the size — it is Conv3d, so the kernels have $27$ and $125$ taps. And multiplying by the input resolution: convolution weights are shared across positions, so the input size never enters. Note it was not even given — that omission is the hint.

Notice where the parameters actually are: layer 2 holds $99.3\%$ of them, because it multiplies the largest kernel by the largest channel product. Kernel volume and channel count multiply, so a $5^3$ kernel on 16 channels is expensive in a way a $3^3$ kernel on 1 channel is not.

explanation:
Answer: batch-all $\mathbf{3{,}000}$; batch-hard $\mathbf{30}$; ratio $\mathbf{100\times}$

Batch size $B = PK = 6 \cdot 5 = 30$.

Batch-all forms every valid triplet: pick any anchor ($B$ ways), any other sample of its class as the positive ($K - 1$ ways), and any sample of a different class as the negative ($B - K$ ways): \[ B(K-1)(B-K) = 30 \cdot 4 \cdot 25 = \mathbf{3{,}000}. \] Batch-hard keeps, per anchor, only the hardest positive and the hardest negative — one triplet each, so $B = \mathbf{30}$. The ratio is $\mathbf{100\times}$.

What the ratio means is the point of the question. Batch-all averages over 3,000 triplets, most of which are easy and contribute zero loss, so the informative signal is diluted; its batch size is a compute knob. Batch-hard keeps 30 extreme triplets, so its batch size is a hardness knob — larger batches mean harder mined negatives, which is why the same parameter has completely different meanings in the two schemes.
stem: A structured batch has $P = 6$ classes and $K = 5$ samples each. How many triplets does batch-all produce, how many does batch-hard, and what is the ratio?

explanation:
What it is. A convolution with $K_{\text{eff}} = 1$: at each spatial position independently, it takes the $C_{\text{in}}$-vector of channel values and applies a learned linear map to produce a $C_{\text{out}}$-vector. It is a fully-connected layer across channels, shared across all positions.

Three uses, and they are the answer.

  1. Change channel depth cheaply — the bottleneck in ResNet, and the projection half of a depthwise separable convolution (Q37).
  2. Mix channel information, which a depthwise or grouped convolution cannot do on its own.
  3. Add depth and non-linearity for almost no parameters, since it costs $C_{\text{in}}C_{\text{out}}$ rather than $K^2 C_{\text{in}}C_{\text{out}}$.

And what it does not do: it does not change the receptive field at all (Q2), and it does not change the spatial resolution.
stem: State what a $1\times1$ convolution does and why it is useful.

explanation:
Training. The whole target sequence is known. Feeding the ground-truth prefix rather than the model's own output does two things: the entire sequence can be processed in parallel in one forward pass (with the causal mask doing the work of hiding the future), and an early mistake cannot poison every later position. Both make training faster and far more stable.

Inference. There is no ground truth — that is what you are trying to produce. The model must consume its own predictions, one token at a time, so generation is inherently sequential.

The consequence worth adding is that this creates a train/test mismatch, usually called exposure bias: at training the model only ever sees correct prefixes, and at inference it must cope with its own imperfect ones, which it was never trained on.
stem: Explain why teacher forcing is used during training but not at inference.

explanation:
Given the corrupted input, MLM predicts each masked position from the same encoder output, independently of the other masked positions. Nothing in the objective couples them.

The concrete case. Mask both tokens of a two-word city name in a context where “New York” and “San Francisco” are equally plausible. The marginal at position 1 splits between {New, San} and the marginal at position 2 between {York, Francisco}. Because the two decisions are independent, the model assigns substantial probability to the cross-products “New Francisco” and “San York” — strings it has never seen and which are jointly absurd, yet each half of which is individually likely.

Why this matters beyond the curiosity: it is a real limitation of a non-autoregressive objective, and it is one of the arguments XLNet and the autoregressive family make against masked pre-training.
stem: BERT's masked-language-model objective treats masked tokens as conditionally independent given the corrupted input. Give one concrete way this can produce an incoherent prediction.

explanation:
The old problem. Anchor-based detectors emit many overlapping boxes per object, because many anchors independently fire on the same thing. NMS is a hand-written post-process that keeps the highest-scoring box and deletes its neighbours — a heuristic outside the network, with its own threshold to tune.

What DETR does instead. The Hungarian algorithm computes a strict one-to-one assignment between the $N$ predictions and the ground-truth objects. Exactly one prediction is matched to each object; every other prediction, including a perfectly good near-duplicate of a matched one, is assigned the “no object” class and trained towards it.

So the mechanism is a change of what is penalised. Duplicate boxes are not filtered out after the fact — they are explicitly punished during training, so the model learns a set-valued output with no duplicates in it. The suppression moved from post-processing into the loss.

Four predictions, two objects. Predictions $\hat y_1$ and $\hat y_2$ are near-duplicates on object 1 — costs $0.9$ and $1.1$, almost tied. The Hungarian algorithm must pick exactly one, so $\hat y_1$ is matched and $\hat y_2$ is trained towards “no object” even though it is a perfectly good box. That is the whole trick: the near-duplicate is not filtered later, it is penalised now.

Two details the question rewards. The matching itself carries no gradient — it is a discrete solver run to fix the assignment, after which the loss is differentiated given that assignment (Q12). And the box loss applies only to matched predictions: the indicator $\mathbf{1}_{\{c_i \ne \varnothing\}}$ switches it off for the unmatched ones, since there is no box to regress towards.
stem: Explain why bipartite matching removes the need for non-maximum suppression.

explanation:
The problem. Regular sparse convolution computes an output wherever the kernel overlaps any active site. With a $3\times3\times3$ kernel, one active voxel therefore produces a $3\times3\times3$ block of active outputs; after $L$ layers the active region is a cube of side $1 + 2L$, containing $(1+2L)^3$ voxels (Q34). The active set grows like $L^3$ while the actual surface it represents has not grown at all — the tensor stops being sparse, and the whole reason for using sparse convolutions evaporates.

The fix. Submanifold sparse convolution restricts the output locations to sites that were already active. It still reads from inactive neighbours (as zeros), so the receptive field grows normally — what does not grow is the active set, which stays exactly fixed layer after layer.

What is lost. If two components are not already connected through active sites, no SSC layer can ever pass information between them: the signal would have to travel through inactive locations, and SSC never writes there. The property that fixes the dilation is precisely the property that blocks communication — they are the same restriction. Real networks therefore interleave striding, pooling, or an occasional regular SC layer to reconnect components, accepting a controlled amount of dilation in exchange.
stem: Regular sparse convolution suffers from the “dilation problem” and submanifold sparse convolution fixes it. State what the problem is, how SSC fixes it, and what capability is lost as a result.

explanation:
What over-smoothing is. A message-passing layer replaces each node's feature with an aggregate over its neighbourhood. Aggregation is averaging, and averaging is a low-pass filter — it removes the high-frequency component of the signal on the graph. Applied repeatedly, features within a connected component converge towards the same vector, and nodes become indistinguishable. Downstream, no classifier can separate what the encoder has made identical.

Why it is a tension and not merely a bug. A GNN layer moves information one hop. Stacking $L$ layers gives each node a receptive field of exactly $L$ hops, and that is the only mechanism available — there is no dilation, no pooling pyramid, no global attention. So if a task needs information from four hops away, you need four layers; and four layers is also four rounds of low-pass filtering.

The three escapes (Q25) all decouple depth from smoothing rather than avoiding it: skip connections let a node keep its own earlier representation; Jumping Knowledge keeps every layer's output so the sharp early features survive to the readout; DropEdge removes edges at random, slowing the mixing per layer.

One knob, two consequences, pulling in opposite directions. Reading left to right, the receptive field grows exactly as you want it to: at $L = 6$ every node sees six hops of context. Reading the colours, the node features converge to a common grey and the graph loses the distinctions the classifier needs. There is no setting of $L$ that gets one without the other, which is why the countermeasures all work by changing the architecture rather than by tuning depth.
stem: Explain over-smoothing, and why it is in tension with the only mechanism a GNN has for increasing its receptive field.

explanation:
Two independent reasons, and a full answer names both.

1. The hardest negative is usually a labelling error. A negative closer to the anchor than the positive is either a genuinely hard case or a mislabelled sample. Across a large dataset the mislabelled ones dominate the extreme tail, so “hardest” reliably selects noise, and the network is trained hardest on exactly the examples that are wrong.

2. Collapse is a stable local minimum, and the arithmetic shows it. Suppose the encoder maps every input to the same point. Then $\mathcal{D}_p = \mathcal{D}_n = 0$ for every triplet, and \[ \mathcal{L} = \max\{0,\ \mathcal{D}_p - \mathcal{D}_n + m\} = \max\{0,\ 0 - 0 + m\} = m . \] A finite, uniform loss of $m$ per triplet — not infinite, and crucially not worse than what hard triplets currently pay, which is $> m$. So from a state dominated by hard negatives, collapsing reduces the loss, and the optimiser will happily go there. Once collapsed, every gradient is zero by symmetry and the network never recovers.

Why semi-hard mining is the standard answer. A semi-hard triplet scores strictly between $0$ and $m$ (Q29), so collapsing to $m$ would make things worse — the gradient does not point that way. Semi-hard negatives are informative enough to learn from and safe enough not to invite collapse.

The two circles are the whole picture: the inner radius is $\mathcal{D}_p$, the outer is $\mathcal{D}_p + m$, and which annulus the negative lands in determines everything. Now compare each region against the collapse value $m$. Train on the red region and collapse looks like an improvement, so the optimiser takes it. Train on the amber region and collapse looks like a regression, so it does not. That comparison is the answer to why semi-hard mining is safe and hardest-negative mining is not.
stem: Why does training only on the hardest negatives risk network collapse? Use the triplet loss to show what a collapsed encoder would score.

explanation:
The problem. In a single-modality Siamese network the two branches share weights, and that is what guarantees both inputs land in the same space — the same function is applied to both. Across modalities this is impossible: an image encoder and a text encoder take different input types and need different architectures, so there is no shared function and nothing structurally forces their outputs to be comparable. Two independently trained encoders would produce two unrelated spaces, and a distance between them would be meaningless.

What replaces weight sharing. The alignment has to come from the objective instead. A contrastive loss over matched pairs — image $i$ with its own caption — pulls the two embeddings of a true pair together and pushes all mismatched pairs apart. The shared space is not built in; it is learned, and it exists only because the loss insists on it.

The consequence worth stating. Because alignment is supplied entirely by the objective, it is only as good as the pairing supervision: the space is aligned exactly on the kinds of pairs the training data contained, and cross-modal retrieval degrades on concepts that were never paired.
stem: An image encoder and a text encoder in a cross-modal retrieval system cannot share weights, yet their outputs must be comparable. Explain the problem and how the training objective solves it.

explanation:
1. A single input axis with positions numbered, drawn once
  2. Layer by layer, the set of input positions feeding one chosen output
  3. $K_{\text{eff}} = 5,\,3,\,7$ marked at L1, L2, L3 — the $7$ at L3 must show the dilation, $3(3-1)+1$
  4. The jump $J$ entering each layer marked: $1$, $1$, $2$
  5. The final span labelled $\mathbf{19}$ positions, from input $0$ to input $18$
  6. L3's three taps drawn spaced three apart, not adjacent — that is what dilation means

Read it upwards. One L3 output has three taps spaced three L2-units apart, so it reads L2 units $0, 3, 6$. Each of those reads three L1 units at stride 2, and each L1 unit reads five inputs. The leftmost input touched is $0$; the rightmost is $14 + 4 = 18$. Span $= 19$.

The written part: padding does not appear anywhere because it changes only where an output sits relative to the input, not how far the output reaches. Two networks differing only in padding have identical receptive fields and different output lengths.
stem: Sketch, for a 1D input, how the receptive field of one output neuron grows through the three-layer stack of Q42. Draw the input axis once and mark, layer by layer, which input positions feed the neuron. Label the effective kernel size and the jump at each layer. Then state in one sentence why padding does not appear anywhere in your sketch.

explanation:
1. An input-embedding box with positional encoding added by an explicit $\oplus$ before the stack
  2. Sub-layer 1 labelled multi-head self-attention
  3. Sub-layer 2 labelled position-wise feed-forward network
  4. Correct order upwards: self-attention $\to$ Add & Norm $\to$ FFN $\to$ Add & Norm
  5. A residual arrow bypassing each sub-layer and rejoining at its Add & Norm
  6. An “$N\times$” mark showing the layer is stacked
  7. Deduct if a triangular mask appears — the encoder is bidirectional

The written part, and it is where the marks are. Each sub-layer is wrapped as $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{SubLayer}(x))$. Self-attention is the one that moves information between positions; the feed-forward network never looks at another token — it transforms each independently with shared weights. So every layer alternates mix, then transform.

Residual connections plus normalisation are there to make depth trainable: the residual gives gradients a path that skips the sub-layer, mitigating vanishing gradients, and the normalisation stabilises the scale of activations and sharply improves convergence time. LayerNorm rather than BatchNorm because it normalises over the feature dimensions of each token independently, making it independent of both batch size and sequence position — which matters when sequences vary in length.
stem: How is a single layer of the Transformer encoder structured? Sketch it and label the important components, including what must be done to the input before it enters the very first layer. Then explain in two or three sentences which of your sub-layers moves information between tokens and which does not, and why both the residual connections and the normalisation are there.

explanation:
1. Block $\ell$: four $4\times4$ windows, partition aligned to the top-left corner
  2. Block $\ell+1$: the same grid partitioned with the boundaries displaced by $\lfloor M/2 \rfloor = 2$ patches in both directions
  3. The displaced partition correctly yields nine regions of unequal size, not four
  4. One patch marked whose window-mates change between the two blocks
  5. Both blocks labelled W-MSA and SW-MSA

The two marked patches are horizontally adjacent and sit either side of the central boundary in block $\ell$, so W-MSA never lets them attend to each other. After the shift they fall inside the same central window and do. That is the entire mechanism: without it, window boundaries would be permanent walls and Swin would be a grid of independent local transformers with no global information flow at all.

What it costs. The shifted partition is irregular — nine regions of three different sizes rather than four equal ones — which would mean padding and wasted compute. Swin avoids that with a cyclic shift of the feature map plus a mask that stops patches attending across the wrap-around, recovering a regular batch of $4\times4$ windows. Complexity stays linear in the number of patches, which is the whole reason for windowing (Q11).
stem: Below are two $8\times8$ patch grids representing the same feature map in two successive Swin blocks, with window size $M = 4$. On the left grid, draw the window partition used by W-MSA. On the right grid, draw the partition used by the following SW-MSA block. Mark one patch that lies in the same window as a given neighbour in one block but a different window in the other, and use it to explain in two sentences what the shift buys and what it costs.

explanation:
1. One active site in an otherwise empty grid, drawn as the starting state
  2. SC after one layer: a $3\times3$ block; after two: $5\times5$ — i.e. side $1+2L$
  3. SSC after one and two layers: still exactly one active site
  4. Both side lengths labelled
  5. A note that SSC still reads from inactive neighbours, so the receptive field grows in both cases — only the active set differs

The problem the top row shows. Regular sparse convolution writes an output wherever the kernel touches an active site, so one voxel becomes a $3\times3$ block, then $5\times5$. In 3D that is $(1+2L)^3$ — $27$ voxels after one layer, $125$ after two, $343$ after three — while the surface being represented has not grown at all. Within a few layers the tensor is dense and the entire point of a sparse representation is gone.

What the bottom row gives up. SSC restricts outputs to already-active sites, so the active set never grows. But that also means information can never reach a location that was not active to begin with — two disconnected components can never communicate, no matter how many SSC layers you stack, because every path between them would have to pass through inactive space. Real networks therefore interleave striding, pooling or an occasional regular SC layer to reconnect components, accepting a controlled dose of dilation in exchange.

The receptive field grows in both rows. SSC still reads from inactive neighbours, treating them as zero — reading was never the problem. It is writing to new locations that destroys sparsity.
stem: A single active site sits in an otherwise empty 2D grid. Sketch the set of active sites after one layer and after two layers, for (i) regular sparse convolution with a $3\times3$ kernel and (ii) submanifold sparse convolution with the same kernel. Label the side length of the active region in each case. Then state, in one sentence each, the problem your first sketch demonstrates and the capability your second sketch gives up.

explanation:
1. The same five elements drawn three times, in the same arrangement
  2. Deep sets: no edges at all between elements
  3. GNN: edges only where the given graph has them — a sparse subset
  4. Transformer: every pair connected, i.e. the complete graph
  5. All three labelled, and the ordering most-to-least constrained made explicit

What a GNN buys over deep sets. Deep sets has no edges, so it can only ever compute a function of the multiset of node features: two graphs with identical features and completely different connectivity give identical outputs (Q24). A GNN reads the edges, so structure enters the computation — that is the whole difference, and it is why deep sets is not a graph neural network despite being permutation invariant.

What a GNN gives up against a transformer. A transformer is a GNN on the complete graph: every element interacts with every other in a single layer, so the maximum path length is $1$. A sparse GNN needs one layer per hop, so distant nodes only communicate after several layers — and stacking those layers is what causes over-smoothing (Q52). The transformer pays for its reach in the other currency: $O(n^2)$ per layer against a GNN's $O(|\mathcal{E}|)$, which is the same trade-off Q8 and Q11 measure.
stem: Draw the same small set of five elements three times, and on each copy draw the interaction pattern permitted by (i) deep sets / PointNet, (ii) a GNN layer on a sparse graph, and (iii) a transformer encoder. Label each. Then use your three pictures to explain what a GNN buys over deep sets and what it gives up against a transformer.

explanation:
1. A message function taking three arguments, including $\mathbf{e}_{ij}$ — that is what “supports edge features” means
  2. An aggregation over $\mathcal{N}(i)$, explicitly marked permutation invariant
  3. An update function combining the node's own feature with the aggregate
  4. A loop over all nodes, with the three stages in that order
  5. The statement of what breaks without invariance
for each node i in V:
    # 1. MESSAGE - one per incident edge, may read the edge feature
    for each j in N(i):
        m_ij = phi(x_i, x_j, e_ij)

    # 2. AGGREGATE - must be PERMUTATION INVARIANT (sum / mean / max)
    a_i = SUM_{j in N(i)} m_ij

    # 3. UPDATE - combine the node's own state with the aggregate
    x_i' = gamma(x_i, a_i)

Step 2 is the one that must be permutation invariant. Steps 1 and 3 are ordinary learned functions applied pointwise — $\phi$ to each edge, $\gamma$ to each node — and neither sees more than one item at a time, so neither can depend on ordering. Only the aggregation looks at a collection, and a collection is exactly where an order could sneak in.

What breaks if it is not invariant. A graph has no canonical node ordering; the neighbours of $i$ arrive in whatever order the data structure happens to store them. If $\bigoplus$ were order-sensitive — concatenation, or an RNN over the neighbour list — then relabelling the nodes would change $a_i$ and therefore the output. The same graph, stored two ways, would produce two different answers. The layer would no longer be permutation equivariant, and the graph-level readout on top of it would no longer be permutation invariant (Q22, Q23), so the model would be learning properties of the storage order rather than of the graph.

The extra mark: name the choice and its consequence. Sum is the most expressive of the three — it can count, so it distinguishes neighbourhoods of different sizes; mean normalises away degree, which helps when degrees vary wildly but throws away exactly that count; max is robust to outliers and is what PointNet uses (Q19).
stem: Write pseudo-code for one message-passing layer that supports edge features, in the general MPNN form. Use $\mathbf{x}_i$ for node features, $\mathbf{e}_{ij}$ for edge features and $\mathcal{N}(i)$ for the neighbourhood. Mark clearly which single step must be permutation invariant, and say in one sentence what breaks if it is not.

explanation:
The four outcomes are graded by how much the combination gives you that you did not already have:

outcomewhat it means
inconclusivethe modalities disagree and you cannot resolve it
dominatedone modality carries everything; the other is dead weight
modulatedone modality adjusts how the other is read
emergenta meaning appears that is in neither modality alone

Only emergent pays for the extra encoder, the extra data and the extra alignment problem. Sarcasm is the standard example: the words say one thing, the tone says another, and the meaning — irony — is in neither channel by itself.
stem: Which outcome of combining two modalities is the one that actually justifies building a multimodal model?
options: inconclusive
dominated
modulated
emergent

explanation:
Fusing at the raw input means concatenating the two signals before any encoder, and then running one network over the result. That only makes sense if a single operation is meaningful on both — same dimensionality, same units, same spatial layout. Two RGB cameras qualify. A camera and a LiDAR point cloud do not: there is no convolution that is simultaneously the right operation on a pixel grid and on an unordered set of $(x,y,z)$ points.

Why (c) is the wrong answer even though it sounds right. Separate encoders per modality are exactly what late and intermediate fusion need. Requiring them would contradict the premise of the question.

The single distinguishing question: how many vectors come out? One $\Rightarrow$ fusion. One per modality $\Rightarrow$ coordination. Everything else — early or late, attention or concatenation — is a detail inside one of these two shapes. This figure answers Q1, Q27 and Q46 at once.

explanation:
Plain bilinear fusion computes the outer product $a\,b^{\!\top}$ and nothing else. Tensor fusion appends a constant $1$ to each modality vector first, and only then takes the outer product. That one change is the whole idea, because the appended $1$ manufactures three extra blocks for free.

Reading it. The single interaction block is surrounded by both unimodal blocks and a constant, so a downstream linear layer can recover the image-only answer, the text-only answer, a bias, or any mixture — without the interaction having to encode them. Plain bilinear fusion has only the blue block, so if one modality is missing or uninformative the product collapses and nothing survives.

4th true, and it is the method's fatal flaw. With $d$-dimensional vectors the two-modality output has $(d+1)^2$ entries; three modalities give $(d+1)^3$. At $d = 128$ that is $129^3 \approx 2.1$ million entries for one fused representation. This is why low-rank factorisations of tensor fusion exist at all.

3rd false. Tensor fusion is a fixed algebraic construction applied to two already pooled vectors. Cross-modal attention aligns sequences — which word attends to which image region. They solve different problems and are routinely used together.

One encoder consumes a pixel grid, the other a token sequence; there is no single set of weights that is defined on both. What CLIP shares is not the weights but the output space — and the contrastive loss is what forces the two separately-parameterised encoders to agree about where things live in it.

Why the 4th sits uneasily beside the 3rd. Zero-shot classification at test time still rests on massive paired supervision at training time — 400 million image–text pairs. “Zero-shot” describes the downstream task, not the pre-training.

3rd is false, and it is the point of the queue. If gradients flowed back through the queue entries you would need the computation graph of every one of them in memory — which is precisely the cost the queue was invented to avoid. Entries are detached feature vectors: cheap, and no longer differentiable.

Which raises the problem the momentum encoder solves. If the key encoder were just the student's weights, then a vector computed five hundred steps ago would have been produced by a very different network, and comparing it to today's query would be meaningless. The EMA update $\theta_k \leftarrow m\,\theta_k + (1-m)\,\theta_q$ with $m \approx 0.999$ makes the key encoder drift slowly enough that the whole queue stays approximately consistent.

The decoupling in one line: SimCLR's number of negatives is its batch size, so buying more negatives means buying more GPU memory. MoCo's number of negatives is the queue length, which costs only the storage of $K$ vectors.

explanation:
This one is genuinely confusing the first time, because the output looks exactly like a classifier's.

The situation. DINO has no labels, so it cannot have classes. But it needs the student and teacher to agree, and to train agreement by gradient descent you need a differentiable measure of disagreement between two outputs.

The trick. Push both outputs through a softmax over $K$ dimensions. Now each is a probability distribution, and cross-entropy between them is a perfectly good loss. The $K$ dimensions are just the coordinates that make this possible — an arbitrary vocabulary the network invents for itself. Nothing says dimension $37$ means “dog”.

The consequence you should be able to state. Because the dimensions are arbitrary, the trivial solution — put everything in dimension $37$ regardless of input — also achieves perfect agreement. That is collapse, and it is why centering and sharpening exist (Q28, Q47, Q57).

Three of the four options are true statements. The question asks which is not a reason for efficiency, and that is a different test.

(a)is a reason, and the dominant one. $49$ tokens instead of $196$; attention is quadratic, so the encoder's attention cost falls by $16\times$ (Q40).
(c)is a reason. The decoder runs on all $196$ tokens, so it would be the new bottleneck if it were not deliberately shallow and narrow. It is thrown away afterwards, so nothing is lost by keeping it small.
(b)is true but is not an efficiency reason. A per-pixel $L_2$ loss over $147$ patches rather than $196$ saves an utterly negligible amount of compute next to a Transformer forward pass. Restricting the loss to masked patches is about the task — scoring the model on patches it could simply copy would let it score well without predicting anything.
(d)is a reason, and a real one. Needing no negatives is why MAE trains at ordinary batch sizes while SimCLR needs $8192$ (Q6).

explanation:
The instinct is to mark all four, because LoRA is “the memory-saving method”. Being precise about which memory it saves is the whole question.

1st, not removed. The frozen weights are still needed for every forward pass. They sit in VRAM exactly as before — LoRA does not shrink the model, it shrinks what you train.

3rd and 4th, removed — and this is where the saving is. A frozen parameter has no gradient and no optimiser state. Adam keeps two states per trainable parameter, so the base model's three companion copies (gradient, first moment, second moment) simply vanish.

2nd, not removed, and this catches people out. Activations must still be stored for the backward pass, because the gradient has to be propagated through the frozen layers to reach adapters sitting deeper in the network. Freezing a weight removes its gradient; it does not remove the need to backpropagate past it.

$7$B parameters at $16$ bits (the arithmetic is Q42). The blue bar is identical in both rows — LoRA never touches it. The $4\times$ figure in Q42 is exactly the ratio between the two rows, and the adapter's own footprint at rank $8$ is too small to see at this scale: $65\,536$ parameters against $7$ billion.

The gradient is with respect to $\mathbf{x}$, not $\theta$. Option (a) is the gradient used in maximum-likelihood training — also called the score in statistics, which is exactly why the distinction has to be made deliberately here.

Dimensionally: $\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\log p$ is a vector living in data space, one component per pixel. That is what makes it usable as a direction to move a sample in.

explanation:
Exactly one option is correct, and it is the one the whole field rests on.

3rd — why score modelling is possible at all. Write the model as $p(\mathbf{x}) = ilde p(\mathbf{x})/Z$. Then \[ abla_{\mathbf{x}}\log p(\mathbf{x}) = abla_{\mathbf{x}} igl[\log ilde p(\mathbf{x}) - \log Z igr] = abla_{\mathbf{x}}\log ilde p(\mathbf{x}), \] because $Z$ is a number, not a function of $\mathbf{x}$, so its gradient is zero. The intractable normaliser is differentiated away.

2nd — false, and the dimension is the giveaway. The score is $ abla_{\mathbf{x}}\log p(\mathbf{x})$: a vector with one component per input dimension, not a scalar. That is exactly what makes it usable as a direction to move a sample in — a scalar could not point anywhere.

4th — false, and it is the subtler trap. The score points uphill locally, in the direction of steepest increase from wherever you are standing. It knows nothing about the global mode: on a bimodal density it points at whichever mode you are nearest, which is precisely why noiseless Langevin dynamics gets stuck (Q18, Q58).

1st — false, and a category error. Integrating to one is a constraint on densities. The score is a vector field; there is no sense in which it integrates to one. That freedom is the second reason it is easy to fit: any $\mathbb{R}^d o \mathbb{R}^d$ network will do.

How to read the pair. The score is zero at exactly three places: both modes and the valley bottom. At a mode the zero is stable — step either way and the score pushes you back. At the valley the zero is unstable — step either way and the score pushes you further away, towards whichever mode you drifted towards. Between mode A and the valley the score is negative, i.e. it points back at mode A; between the valley and mode B it is positive, i.e. it points at mode B.

This one figure answers Q17, Q18 and the sketch in Q58. The numbers are exact for $p(x)\propto e^{-(x+1.5)^2}+0.8\,e^{-(x-1.5)^2}$: modes at $x=\pm1.50$, valley at $x = 0.048$, and $p( ext{valley})/p( ext{mode A}) = 0.045$.

explanation:
The update is \[ \mathbf{x}_{t+1} = \mathbf{x}_t + \tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\,\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\log p(\mathbf{x}_t) + \sqrt{\epsilon}\;\mathbf{z}_t, \qquad \mathbf{z}_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I). \] Delete the last term and what remains is gradient ascent on $\log p$. Gradient ascent is a deterministic optimiser: it climbs to the nearest stationary point and stops.

Look at the figure above. Start anywhere left of the valley and noiseless Langevin walks uphill to mode A and sits there forever. It will never visit mode B, never produce a sample from the tail, and never produce two different outputs from the same start. You get the mode, not the distribution — and a generative model that always returns the single most likely image is useless.

The noise is therefore not numerical hygiene; it is the entire difference between optimisation and sampling. It is also what carries a sample across the valley, since the score there points the wrong way.

Why (b) is wrong. In the tails the score points strongly inwards (see the green curve at $x = \pm 3$), so the iteration is self-correcting, not divergent.

explanation:
Write the update as a base point plus a correction: \[ \tilde\varepsilon = \underbrace{\varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,\varnothing)}_{\text{unconditional}} + \gamma\underbrace{\bigl(\varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,c) - \varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,\varnothing)\bigr)}_{\text{the ``direction of the condition''}} \] 1st true. A single network is trained with the condition randomly dropped (say $10\%$ of the time), so it learns both the conditional and the unconditional score. No separate classifier is trained, and none has to be made robust to noisy inputs — which was the awkward part of classifier guidance.

2nd true, and this is the practical appeal. $\gamma$ appears only at sampling time, so fidelity can be traded against diversity per sample, with no retraining.

3rd true — substitute. At $\gamma = 1$ the expression telescopes to $\varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,c)$ exactly. So $\gamma = 1$ is “no guidance, just conditioning”; $\gamma = 0$ discards the condition entirely (Q43); $\gamma > 1$ extrapolates past the conditional score, which is what sharpens prompt adherence and, pushed too far, produces the over-saturated look.

4th true, and it is what makes the 1st possible. Dropping the condition at random during training — typically about $10\%$ of examples — is the entire training-time change. It is what leaves one network able to produce both scores, and therefore what removes the separate classifier.

And note the cost, which no option states: both $\varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,c)$ and $\varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,\varnothing)$ must be evaluated at every sampling step — two forward passes, so guided sampling costs twice as much (Q43).

NeRF keeps only the first two — a point along the ray blocks light (density $\sigma$) and adds light (colour $\mathbf{c}$). Both scattering terms are dropped because they couple different rays to each other, and once rays are coupled you can no longer render one pixel independently of the rest of the image. Independence per ray is what makes the whole method trainable.

explanation:
\[ T(t) = \exp\!\left(-\int_{t_n}^{t}\sigma(\mathbf{r}(s))\,\mathrm{d}s\right) \] Every option is true, and the 2nd is the one the formula settles. $\sigma \ge 0$, so the integral is non-decreasing in $t$, so its negative exponential is non-increasing. A dropping density makes $T$ stop falling; it cannot make $T$ rise. Physically: light already absorbed does not come back.

1st is the definition. $T(t)$ is the probability that a ray entering at $t_n$ has not been absorbed by the time it reaches $t$.

3rd is the same fact from the other side. Where $\sigma = 0$ nothing is added to the integral, so $T$ is flat — empty space is free.

4th. $T(t)$ is the probability of getting as far as $t$; $\sigma(t)\,dt$ is the probability of being stopped in the next stretch given that you got there. Their product is the probability of terminating at $t$, and it is exactly the weight $w(t) = T(t)\,\sigma(t)$ that multiplies the colour in the rendering integral. The weights form a proper distribution along the ray, which is what makes hierarchical sampling possible: sample where the weight is large.

Three stacked panels, one story. $T$ can only fall. It is flat through empty space, collapses through the object, and is then pinned near zero forever — so the weight $w = T\sigma$ is large only in the thin shell where $\sigma$ has just turned on while $T$ is still high. Samples behind the object have a perfectly good $\sigma$ but are multiplied by $T \approx 0$, so they are invisible. This is also the answer to Q59, which asks you to draw it.

Filled in: In DINO the teacher's weights are an exponential moving average of the student's, and a stop-gradient is applied to the teacher branch. Centering prevents collapse onto a fixed, non-uniform (always the same peak) teacher distribution; sharpening prevents collapse onto a uniform one. The second half is the one people reverse. Centering fights the fixed non-uniform failure — every input landing on the same one or two output dimensions. Sharpening fights the uniform failure — every output flat, carrying no information at all.

The reliable way to remember which is which: centering flattens, so it must be fighting a peak; sharpening peaks, so it must be fighting flatness. Each mechanism causes the very failure the other one prevents, which is why neither works alone and both are present. See the figure at Q57.

Filled in: The InfoNCE bound on mutual information is $\mathrm{MI} \ge \mathbf{\log N} - \mathcal{L}$, so the number of candidates sets a hard ceiling (an upper bound the method cannot exceed however well it trains). Here $N$ is the number of candidates: one positive plus $N-1$ negatives.

Read the inequality carefully, because it is the reverse of the usual intuition. The loss $\mathcal{L}$ is non-negative, so the bound can never exceed $\log N$. Even a perfect contrastive model with $\mathcal{L} = 0$ certifies only $\log N$ nats of mutual information. At $N = 8192$ that is $\ln 8192 = 9.01$ nats, or $13$ bits.

So a batch or queue of $8192$ can never demonstrate more than $13$ bits of shared information, however good the representation actually is — and this is the formal reason contrastive methods keep reaching for larger $N$. It is also the reason MoCo's queue was such an effective idea (Q6): it raises $N$ without raising the batch size.

Filled in: The trade-off between learning new tasks and retaining old ones is called the stability–plasticity dilemma. The four families of continual learning method are regularisation-based, replay-based, optimisation-based and architecture-based. The four families again, with the one-line distinction that separates them:

regularisationpenalise moving parameters that mattered before; store no old data (EWC, LwF)
replaystore, or generate, some old data and keep training on it
optimisationconstrain the gradient — project updates so they cannot increase loss on old tasks (GEM)
architecturegive each task its own parameters: new branches, masks, or adapters

Filled in: In the SDE $\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x} = f(\mathbf{x},t)\,\mathrm{d}t + g(t)\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{w}$, the term $f$ is the drift, the term $g$ is the diffusion term, and $\mathbf{w}$ is a Wiener process (Brownian motion). DDPM corresponds to the variance-preserving choice and NCSN to the variance-exploding one. The drift $f$ is the deterministic pull; the diffusion term $g$ sets how much noise is injected; a Wiener process is Brownian motion, whose increments are independent Gaussians with variance proportional to $\mathrm{d}t$.

The names describe the dashed green curve. VP shrinks the signal as it adds noise, so the total variance is held at $1$ — $f$ is a decay term pulling $\mathbf{x}$ towards zero, and $\mathbf{x}_T$ ends up as standard Gaussian noise. VE leaves the data alone and piles noise on top, so the variance runs away to $\sigma_{\max}^2$ — $f = 0$, and $\mathbf{x}_T$ is the data drowned in enormous noise. Both destroy the data; the difference is whether the scale is held fixed, and that is what the two names are recording.

The density must not depend on the viewing direction, because geometry is a property of the scene, not of the camera — otherwise the reconstruction is not multi-view consistent. Five inputs, four outputs: $(x,y,z,\theta,\phi) \mapsto (\sigma, \mathbf{c})$. The restriction on $\sigma$ is not a simplification but a deliberate inductive bias, and it is unpacked at length in Q53.

explanation: The logic chain: you want $w(x) = p_{\text{target}}(x)/p_{\text{source}}(x)$, but you cannot evaluate either density. A classifier trained to tell source from target gives you the ratio for free, because \[ \frac{1 - c(\text{src}\mid x)}{c(\text{src}\mid x)} = \frac{p(\text{tgt}\mid x)}{p(\text{src}\mid x)} \;\propto\; \frac{p_{\text{target}}(x)}{p_{\text{source}}(x)} \] by Bayes, with the class priors absorbed into the constant. So: train the discriminator, convert its output into weights, apply the weights, and only then train the thing you actually wanted. Steps (c) and (d) are throwaway machinery in service of (a).
