very little — a high likelihood is not a membership test
it is an outlier

explanation:
Take the reverse-time SDE and drop the noise term, adjusting the drift to compensate: \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}}{\mathrm{d}t} = f(\mathbf{x},t) - \tfrac12 g(t)^2\,\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\log p_t(\mathbf{x}). \] The result has the same marginals at every $t$ as the stochastic process, and it is deterministic. Everything else follows from that one sentence.

1st — determinism buys an invertible map. Each noise vector corresponds to exactly one image and the correspondence can be run in either direction, so you can encode a real image to its latent, interpolate between two latents, and decode. A stochastic sampler gives a different image every time and has no such map.

2nd — it is an ordinary ODE. That means Runge–Kutta, adaptive step sizes, and forty years of numerical analysis, none of which was written with diffusion in mind and all of which applies.

3rd — and this is where the speed comes from. A good solver takes large steps where the trajectory is smooth. Modern samplers reach comparable quality in $20$–$50$ evaluations against DDPM's many hundreds.

4th — and this is the structural point. $s_\theta$ was trained to answer one local question: what noise is in this input, at this level? It was never told how sampling would proceed. Training and sampling are decoupled, so a better solver is a drop-in replacement and no retraining is involved — which is why the sampler literature moved so much faster than the training literature.
stem: Mark all that are true of the probability flow ODE:
options: it is deterministic, so latents can be interpolated and the map inverted
off-the-shelf numerical solvers can be used on it
steps can be skipped, so far fewer network evaluations are needed
it uses the same trained score network as the stochastic sampler, with no retraining

explanation:
“Pose” in ordinary usage means where something is and which way it is facing — six degrees of freedom, $(x,y,z)$ plus pitch, yaw and roll. Those are the extrinsics. A calibrated pose adds the intrinsics: focal length, principal point, and the distortion parameters.

Why the intrinsics cannot be left out. The whole purpose is to convert a pixel into a ray in world space, and the first step of that conversion is \[ \mathbf{d}_{\text{cam}} = \Bigl(\tfrac{u-c_x}{f},\ \tfrac{v-c_y}{f},\ 1\Bigr), \] which uses the focal length and the principal point and nothing else. Only then do the extrinsics rotate that direction into the world. Without $f$ you do not know how wide the camera's cone of vision is — the same pixel is a different ray on a wide-angle lens and a telephoto — so you cannot triangulate, and multi-view consistency has nothing to be consistent about.

Where they come from in practice. Structure from motion, usually COLMAP, which recovers poses and intrinsics together and hands back a sparse point cloud as a by-product. Note the field of view falls out of the same numbers: $\mathrm{FoV} = 2\arctan\bigl((W/2)/f\bigr)$.
stem: A calibrated pose, as the lecture uses the term, includes:
options: position, orientation and the camera intrinsics
position only
position and orientation only
the intrinsics only

explanation:
The 3rd is the case for the approach. Rolling out a policy inside a learned model is cheap (no robot, no reset, no wall-clock), safe (a crash costs nothing), and sample-efficient in the sense that matters — a small amount of real experience is amortised over a very large number of imagined trajectories.

The 4th is the qualification, and the 1st is the mistake it corrects. Imagination removes the real interaction needed to train the controller. It does not remove the real interaction needed to build the model: $V$ and $M$ have to be fitted to observations that came from somewhere. This is why the training is staged — collect experience, fit the world model, then train the controller inside it, and usually iterate, because a policy that has improved visits states the model has never seen.

The 2nd is false and mixes up the two systems. PlaNet plans in latent space with model predictive control, re-planning at every step — online search. Dreamer learns an explicit policy and value function inside the imagination, so at execution time it simply acts, with no search at all. That difference is the reason Dreamer is the one that scales.

And note which components form the world model: $V$ (the encoder) and $M$ (the dynamics) only. $C$ is the policy trained inside it, not a part of it.
stem: Mark all that are true of training a policy inside a learned world model:
options: it removes the need for real interaction entirely
Dreamer works by planning with online search at every step
it is cheaper, safer and more sample-efficient than acting in the world
real interaction is still needed to collect the data that trains the model itself

explanation:
Filled in: An RNN's state update is $a^{(t)} = \mathbf{b + Wh^{(t-1)} + Ux^{(t)}}$ and $h^{(t)} = \mathbf{\tanh(a^{(t)})}$. Unrolling puts the product of $\mathbf{\partial h^{(k)}/\partial h^{(k-1)}}$ into the gradient, which behaves like $\mathbf{\gamma^{t}}$. A factor below $1$ gives vanishing gradients and a factor above $1$ gives exploding gradients; the standard remedy for the second is gradient clipping. Why the same matrix appears once per step, and why that is the whole problem. Backpropagation through time differentiates a composition of $t$ copies of the same function, so the chain rule produces \[ \prod_{k=1}^{t}\frac{\partial h^{(k)}}{\partial h^{(k-1)}} = \prod_{k=1}^{t}\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\tanh'(a^{(k)})\bigr)W \;\sim\; \gamma^{t}. \] A product of $t$ near-identical factors is an exponential in $t$. There is no middle ground: unless $\gamma$ sits almost exactly at $1$, the gradient either dies or blows up, and it does so at a rate that makes the difference between $t=10$ and $t=100$ absolute.

Why $\tanh$ and not something unbounded. It keeps the state in $[-1,1]$, so the forward pass stays stable however long the sequence. The cost is $\tanh' \le 1$, with equality only at $0$ — so the diagonal factor is a contraction almost everywhere, and vanishing is the common case.

Why the two failures need different remedies, which is the trap. Exploding gradients are a scale problem: the direction is informative and only the magnitude is wrong, so rescaling the gradient to a fixed norm fixes it completely and costs nothing. Vanishing gradients are an information problem: the signal from step $t-100$ has been multiplied into numerical nothing, and there is no scaling that recovers what is no longer there. That is why the cure is architectural — LSTM and GRU gating provide an additive path along which the state can travel without being multiplied by $W$ at every step. Truncated BPTT is a third thing again, a memory remedy, not a gradient one.

explanation:
Filled in: Swin's patch merging concatenates each $2\times2$ neighbourhood, multiplying the channels by 4, then a linear projection divides them by 2. So $(H,W,C) \to \mathbf{(H/2,\ W/2,\ 2C)}$, and the shift between successive blocks is $\lfloor M/2 \rfloor$ patches. Follow the channels through, because the two factors are easy to conflate. Concatenating four neighbouring patch vectors of width $C$ gives one vector of width $4C$ — no information is lost, it has only been rearranged from space into channels. The linear projection then halves it to $2C$. Net effect: a quarter of the positions, twice the width.

Why that particular trade. It is the same one a CNN makes at every stage boundary, and for the same reason: as the spatial resolution falls, each remaining position stands for more of the image and needs more capacity to describe it. Doing this repeatedly is what gives Swin a multi-scale feature hierarchy — which a plain ViT does not have, and which is why Swin works as a detection and segmentation backbone where ViT needs help.

Why the shift is half a window and not something else. The point of shifting is that patches separated by a window boundary in one block must share a window in the next. $\lfloor M/2\rfloor$ is the displacement that puts the old boundary through the middle of a new window, which is the largest possible improvement; a smaller shift would leave patches near the centre of the old window still grouped together, and a shift of $M$ would reproduce the original partition exactly.

explanation:
Filled in: With $\tilde A = \mathbf{A + I}$ and $\tilde D$ the degree matrix of $\tilde A$, the GCN layer is \[ H^{(l+1)} = \mathbf{\sigma\bigl(\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A\tilde D^{-1/2}H^{(l)}W^{(l)}\bigr)}. \] $L$ layers give an $L$-hop receptive field, and typical depth is 2–3 layers because of over-smoothing. Read the layer as three steps. Select the neighbourhood, including the node itself ($\tilde A = A+I$); propagate, scaled by degree ($\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A\tilde D^{-1/2}$); aggregate and apply the non-linearity. Per node: \[ \mathbf{h}^{(l+1)}_i = \sigma\!\left(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)\cup\{i\}} \frac{\mathbf{h}^{(l)}_j W^{(l)}}{\sqrt{\tilde D_{ii}\tilde D_{jj}}}\right). \] Why the self-loop is not optional. Without $I$, a node's new representation is built entirely from its neighbours and it loses itself — $AX$ has no term for $\mathbf{x}_i$. That is plainly wrong for node classification, where the node's own features are usually the strongest evidence. And $\tilde D$ must be built from $\tilde A$, not from $A$; see Q11.

Why depth is the tension of the whole lecture. Each layer extends the receptive field by one hop, so reaching a node three edges away requires three layers. Each layer also averages a node with its neighbours, and repeated averaging converges — under symmetric normalisation towards something proportional to $\sqrt{\deg+1}$, so the representations end up encoding degree and nothing else. Depth is simultaneously the only source of range and the cause of collapse, which is why GCNs are two or three layers deep where a CNN is fifty.

explanation:
Filled in: Additive fusion is $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{w_1\mathbf{x}_A + w_2\mathbf{x}_B}$; element-wise fusion is $\mathbf{\mathbf{w}(\mathbf{x}_A \odot \mathbf{x}_B)}$, in which feature $i$ meets feature $i$. Bilinear fusion is $\mathbf{W(\mathbf{x}_A^{\top}\!\cdot\mathbf{x}_B)}$, in which every feature meets every feature. Concatenating two vectors and applying one linear layer is secretly additive fusion. The ladder is ordered by how much interaction each rung permits, and each step up costs parameters.

Additive lets each modality vote with a fixed weight. It can never express “what this image means depends on the caption”, because the contributions are decided in advance.

Element-wise multiplies, so one modality can gate the other — but only channel by channel, feature $i$ against feature $i$. That presumes the two feature spaces are aligned index by index, which is a strong and usually unearned assumption.

Bilinear forms the full outer product, so every pair interacts. Expressive, and quadratic in the dimensions.

Tensor fusion appends a $1$ to each vector first, which recovers the unimodal terms and a bias alongside the bimodal ones.

The last blank is the one that catches people, and it is worth verifying rather than believing. Concatenate and apply $W$: \[ W\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}_A\\\mathbf{x}_B\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}W_A & W_B\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}_A\\\mathbf{x}_B\end{bmatrix} = W_A\mathbf{x}_A + W_B\mathbf{x}_B . \] It splits. “Concatenate and put an MLP on top” feels like fusion and is additive fusion with learned weights — the first non-linearity does mix them, but the fusion operation itself does not. If you want interaction you have to multiply somewhere.

explanation:
Filled in: LoRA writes $W + \Delta W \approx \mathbf{W + BA}$, with $B \in \mathbf{\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}}$ and $A \in \mathbf{\mathbb{R}^{r\times d}}$. The layer computes $\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{W\mathbf{x} + \tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA\mathbf{x}}$. It is initialised with $A$ random and $B$ zero, so that $\Delta W$ is exactly zero at step $0$; the compression ratio is $d/2r$. The hypothesis, stated plainly. Fine-tuning is the addition of some $\Delta W$. LoRA assumes that for a well pre-trained model this update has low intrinsic rank — that adapting to a new task moves the weights within a low-dimensional subspace rather than everywhere. If so, $\Delta W = BA$ with $r \ll d$ loses little, and costs $2dr$ instead of $d^2$.

Why there is no inference penalty. $BA$ is a $d\times d$ matrix once multiplied out, so after training you can fold it in: $W' = W + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA$, and deploy a single weight matrix. That is a real advantage over adapters, which insert extra layers and therefore extra latency at every forward pass. It also means task switching costs only the swapping of a small pair of matrices.

Where it is applied, in practice: the projection matrices of the transformer's self-attention layers.

Two traps, both about $\alpha$ and $r$. They are not independent — the update is scaled by $\alpha/r$, so raising $r$ while holding $\alpha$ fixed makes each update weaker, and a rank sweep that does not adjust $\alpha$ is measuring two things at once. And $d/2r$ is a ratio of trainable parameters, not of memory; see Q54 of Exam 04 for why the VRAM saving is about $4\times$ rather than $d/2r$.

explanation:
Filled in: Classifier-based guidance uses Bayes to write $s(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{s(\mathbf{x})} + \mathbf{\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\log p(\mathbf{c}\mid\mathbf{x})}$. Classifier-free guidance instead computes $s_\gamma(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{(1-\gamma)s(\mathbf{x}) + \gamma\,s(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{c})}$, which for $\gamma>1$ is extrapolation rather than interpolation, at the cost of two network evaluations per step. Where the first line comes from. Take logs of $p(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{c}) \propto p(\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{c}\mid\mathbf{x})$ and differentiate with respect to $\mathbf{x}$; the normalising constant is independent of $\mathbf{x}$ and disappears, as always. So a conditional score is an unconditional score plus the gradient of a classifier — which is a genuinely elegant result, and it is why the technique was tried first.

Why it was abandoned anyway. That classifier has to be trained on noisy inputs, at every noise level the sampler will visit, because that is what it will be evaluated on. And its class list fixes what you can condition on, which rules out free text. Both restrictions are structural, not engineering problems.

What classifier-free guidance does instead. Train one network with the conditioning sometimes replaced by a learned null token $\mathbf{c}_\varnothing$, so the same weights provide both $s(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{c})$ and $s(\mathbf{x})$. Then form the combination above. No classifier, any conditioning signal, and $\gamma$ is a test-time knob that needs no retraining. The price is two forward passes per sampling step — which is cheaper overall than training and running a separate noisy classifier, but is not cheaper per step, and that distinction is a standard exam trap.

explanation:
Three sub-layers, in a fixed order, each wrapped as $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{SubLayer}(x))$; the option list names only the last of the three wrappers.

Why masked self-attention has to come first. The decoder must first work out what it has already produced before it can ask the encoder anything sensible. The mask sets scores for future positions to $-\infty$ before the softmax — $-\infty$ rather than $0$ because the masking happens in score space, and setting a score to zero would still leave $e^0 = 1$ of weight on a token that has not been generated. This is what allows an entire target sequence to be trained on in one parallel pass without the model reading its own answer.

Why cross-attention is second. $Q$ comes from the decoder, $K$ and $V$ from the encoder. So the query is “given what I have written so far, what in the source is relevant?” — a question that only has an answer once the first sub-layer has summarised what has been written. Note the asymmetry of where $Q$, $K$ and $V$ come from; writing it the other way round is the standard error.

Then the feed-forward network, then the wrapper. The FFN is where the token's own representation is transformed, after all the gathering is done; the encoder has two sub-layers in the same pattern and this is the third.
stem: Order the operations of one original-transformer decoder layer:
items: the residual addition and layer norm that closes the feed-forward sub-layer
masked self-attention over the tokens produced so far
cross-attention, with queries from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder
the position-wise feed-forward network

explanation:
Sample, group, encode, pool — PointNet++ in four words. It is a PointNet applied to a neighbourhood instead of to the whole cloud, and repeating it is what gives the hierarchy PointNet lacked.

Sampling first, by farthest point sampling, not at random. Random sampling draws in proportion to density, so a LiDAR scan yields nearly all its centroids from the near field. FPS spreads them by geometry. It costs $O(NS)$ against $O(1)$, and the coverage is worth it.

Grouping by a ball query, not by $k$NN. A fixed radius gives a fixed physical scale, so “the neighbourhood” means the same thing in a dense region and a sparse one. $k$NN would silently expand to metres in sparse regions and shrink to centimetres in dense ones — the network would be looking at a different-sized object depending on where it stood.

Then the shared MLP per point, then the max pool per group. This pair is exactly PointNet's recipe, applied within the group: a shared map keeps it equivariant, a symmetric reduction makes the group's output invariant to the order its members were listed in. Reversing them — pooling before the MLP — would destroy the per-point information before it had been used.

Where the variants sit: MSG concatenates several radii at the same layer, MRG combines several abstraction levels, and input point dropout during training is what makes the result robust to sampling density.
stem: Order one PointNet++ set-abstraction layer:
items: group the neighbours of each centroid with a ball query
choose the centroids by farthest point sampling
max pool within each group
apply a shared MLP to every point of every group

explanation:
The batch is constructed before anything is embedded, and it is constructed structurally: $P$ classes with $K$ samples each, so every anchor is guaranteed $K-1$ positives. Sampling uniformly at random would leave most anchors with no positive at all and most of the step wasted — see Q14.

Embed the whole batch once. $B = PK$ forward passes, and every triplet is then formed from vectors you already have. This is why online mining is affordable: the expensive part is shared across all $O(B^3)$ possible triplets.

Then select, and note which extreme goes on each side. The hardest positive is the one furthest away; the hardest negative is the one nearest. Both are the cases the current embedding handles worst, which is what “hard” means — but they point in opposite directions along the distance axis and writing one of them backwards is easy.

Then the loss. One triplet per anchor, $B$ in total, and because each was chosen to be the hardest available, almost all of them are active rather than clipped to zero by the hinge. That is the efficiency argument for batch-hard over batch-all, which forms far more triplets of which most contribute nothing (Q45).
stem: Order one training step with online batch-hard mining:
items: compute the triplet loss and backpropagate
embed every sample in the batch
sample a structured batch of $P$ classes with $K$ samples each
for each anchor, take the furthest positive and the nearest negative

explanation:
The ray comes from the pose, and this is the step that needs the intrinsics (Q29): $\mathbf{d}_{\text{cam}} = ((u-c_x)/f,\ (v-c_y)/f,\ 1)$, then rotate into the world. The ray is $\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}$.

Then sample along it, jittered. Divide $[t_n,t_f]$ into $N$ bins and draw one sample uniformly inside each. The jitter is not a numerical nicety: with fixed depths the network only ever sees the same $N$ positions along each ray and can become a lookup table at those positions, leaving the field between them unconstrained. Random offsets force it to be a genuinely continuous function of position, which is what you are actually training.

Query the MLP for $(\mathbf{c},\sigma)$ at each sample. Note the asymmetry: $\sigma$ depends on position only, $\mathbf{c}$ on position and view direction. Whether something is there cannot depend on where you look from; what colour it appears can.

Then composite. $\hat C = \sum_i T_i\alpha_i\mathbf{c}_i$ with $T_i = \prod_{j

The supervision is only the pixel colour — there is no 3D ground truth anywhere in the loop. Geometry emerges because a single density field has to explain every training view at once, and multi-view consistency is a strong enough constraint to pin it down.

items: composite the samples by alpha blending
cast a ray through the pixel from the calibrated camera pose
query the MLP at each sample for its colour and density
draw jittered samples along the ray

FamilyMethodsFree space?Quantised?
dense voxelVoxNet, ScanNet, ScanComplete5151
hierarchicalOctNet, OGN5151
sparseSC/SSC, Minkowski Enginepartial51

The two columns on the right are the whole taxonomy in miniature, and they explain why no family wins. Representing free space — knowing that a region was observed and is empty — is exactly what completion and mapping need, and it is what point clouds cannot do: a point cloud says where surfaces are and is silent about everywhere else. Quantisation is the opposite ledger: grids snap coordinates and lose sub-voxel precision, points do not.

Read the list as a chain of failures rather than four options. Dense grids are simple and cubic; hierarchies make empty space cheap but not free; sparse convolutions make it free and keep quantisation; point-based methods drop the grid and lose free space and accuracy; projection sidesteps 3D and loses geometry. See Q51.

explanation:
All four exist because of one obstacle: normalisation. A network cannot simply output $p_\theta(\mathbf{x})$, because forcing it to integrate to one over all of data space is intractable. Each family is a different way around that, and the taxonomy is really a list of evasions.

Autoregressive factorises: $p(\mathbf{x}) = \prod_i p(x_i\mid\mathbf{x}_{1:i-1})$. Each conditional is over a single variable, often a categorical one, so that normalisation is a softmax and is trivial. The price is sequential generation.

Latent variable pushes the difficulty into a variable you never observe: sample $\mathbf{z}$ from a fixed prior, then $\mathbf{x}$ from $p(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})$. The prior is chosen, so it needs no normalising, and $h \ll d$ gives a compressed bottleneck.

Flow-based makes the map deterministic and invertible, with $h = d$, so the change-of-variables formula gives the exact density from the prior and a Jacobian determinant. The constraint that every layer be invertible with a tractable determinant is severe.

Energy-based writes $p = \frac1Z e^{-\beta E}$: the exponential guarantees positivity and $Z$ guarantees normalisation — and $Z$ is exactly the intractable object. This is the family the score sidesteps entirely, by differentiating $\log p$ with respect to $\mathbf{x}$ so that $\nabla\log Z = 0$.

The distinction worth keeping is flow against latent-variable: a flow transports a sample deterministically, a latent-variable model samples from a conditional. Same diagram, different arrow.
stem: Write next to each family of generative model the letter of its defining property:
pool: deterministic and invertible, with latent dimension equal to the data dimension
the density factorises into a product of conditionals
draw $\mathbf{z}$ from a fixed prior, then $\mathbf{x}$ from $p(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})$, with $h \ll d$

explanation:
Answer: $d_k = \mathbf{64}$; $\mathbf{1.34\times10^{8}} + \mathbf{1.68\times10^{7}} = \mathbf{1.51\times10^{8}}$

\[\begin{aligned} d_k &= d/h = 512/8 = 64 \\[2pt] 4nd^2 &= 4 \cdot 128 \cdot 512^2 = 4\cdot 128 \cdot 262{,}144 = 134{,}217{,}728 \\[2pt] 2n^2d &= 2 \cdot 128^2 \cdot 512 = 2 \cdot 16{,}384 \cdot 512 = 16{,}777{,}216 \\[2pt] C &= 150{,}994{,}944 \approx 1.51\times10^{8} \end{aligned}\]

The projections dominate, by a factor of $8$, and the reason is the same inequality the lecture's cost table turns on. The projection term is $O(nd^2)$ and the attention term is $O(n^2d)$; their ratio is $d/n = 512/128 = 4$, and with the constants $4$ and $2$ it comes to $8$. Since $n < d$, the quadratic-in-$n$ part is not where the time goes.

Which is worth sitting with, because it is the opposite of the usual story. At $n = 128$ “attention is quadratic” is true and irrelevant — you would speed this layer up by shrinking $d$, not by approximating the attention. The quadratic term only overtakes at $n \approx 4d = 2048$. Efficient-attention methods are answers to long sequences and high-resolution images, and applying them to short ones optimises the smaller number.

One more property of this formula. $h$ does not appear. With $hd_k = hd_v = d$, the per-head work shrinks exactly as fast as the number of heads grows, so multi-head attention costs the same as single-head attention at full width. What you buy with $h$ is $h$ independent attention distributions, and the ability to aggregate several low-rank maps into a higher-rank one — not more or less compute.
stem: A transformer layer has $d = 512$, $h = 8$ heads and a sequence of $n = 128$. Using $C = 4nd^2 + 2n^2d$, give $d_k$, both terms of $C$, the total, and say which term dominates and why.

explanation:
Answer: $L = \mathbf{11}$; side $\mathbf{23}$, $\mathbf{12{,}167}$ voxels

A regular sparse convolution writes an output wherever the kernel touches an active site, so a single active voxel grows by one kernel radius per layer: \[ s_L = 1 + L(k-1) = 1 + 2L, \qquad \text{active sites} = s_L^{\,3}. \]

$L$side $s_L$active voxels
$1$$3$$27$
$5$$11$$1{,}331$
$10$$21$$9{,}261$
$\mathbf{11}$$\mathbf{23}$$\mathbf{12{,}167}$

$L=10$ gives $9{,}261$, just short; $L=11$ is the first to exceed $10{,}000$.

What the number is for. It quantifies the dilation problem. Eleven layers is nothing — a shallow network by any modern standard — and one active voxel has already become twelve thousand. Every one of them is a location the layer must now compute at, and almost all of them hold features diluted with zeros. Sparsity, which was the entire reason for using a sparse convolution, is gone before the network is deep enough to be useful.

The contrast that makes the point. A submanifold sparse convolution leaves the active set unchanged at every depth: the count stays $1$ at layer $11$ and at layer $100$. Its cost is that disconnected components can never communicate (Q10 of Exam 04), which is why real networks alternate — mostly submanifold, with a strided or regular layer inserted deliberately when the active set needs to grow.

A companion figure worth carrying: filling a $64^3$ grid from a centred voxel needs $1+2L \ge 64$, so $L \ge 31.5$, i.e. $32$ layers.
stem: A single active voxel is passed through regular sparse convolutions with $k=3$ in 3D. After how many layers does the active region first exceed $10{,}000$ voxels? Give the side length and the count at that layer.

explanation:
Answer: $B = \mathbf{128}$; $\mathbf{107{,}520}$ against $\mathbf{128}$; ratio $\mathbf{840}$

\[\begin{aligned} B &= PK = 16 \cdot 8 = 128 \\[2pt] \text{batch-all} &= B(K-1)(B-K) = 128 \cdot 7 \cdot 120 = 107{,}520 \\[2pt] \text{batch-hard} &= B = 128 \\[2pt] \text{ratio} &= 107{,}520 / 128 = 840 \end{aligned}\]

Read the formula rather than memorising it. For each of the $B$ anchors there are $K-1 = 7$ other samples of its own class to serve as the positive, and $B - K = 120$ samples of other classes to serve as the negative. Multiply.

Why the $840\times$ difference does not translate into $840\times$ the learning. Most of those hundred thousand triplets are easy — the negative already satisfies the margin, the hinge clips the loss to exactly zero, and the gradient contribution is nothing. They cost arithmetic and contribute no signal, and as training progresses the proportion that are useless only grows. Batch-hard forms one triplet per anchor and picks the hardest available each time, so almost every one of its $128$ is active.

And why that makes batch size mean something different in each. For batch-all a larger batch means cubically more triplets — a compute knob. For batch-hard the count stays at $B$ but the hardest negative is drawn from a larger pool, so the triplets get harder — a hardness knob. Turn it too far and you are mining label noise and near-duplicates, whose loss cannot be reduced by learning, and the optimiser takes the collapse instead. Hence the standing advice: batch-all if unsure, batch-hard only at moderate batch size.
stem: A structured batch holds $P = 16$ classes with $K = 8$ samples each. Give the batch size, the number of triplets batch-all produces, the number batch-hard produces, and the ratio.

explanation:
Answer: $\mathbf{5.08\times10^{7}}$, then $\mathbf{1.04\times10^{11}}$ — a factor of $\mathbf{2049}$

\[\begin{aligned} \text{two modalities} &= (128+1)(768+1) \cdot 512 = 129 \cdot 769 \cdot 512 \\ &= 99{,}201 \cdot 512 = 50{,}790{,}912 \approx 5.08\times10^{7} \\[4pt] \text{plus video} &= 50{,}790{,}912 \cdot (2048+1) = 104{,}070{,}578{,}688 \approx 1.04\times10^{11} \end{aligned}\]

Do not miss the $+1$s. They are what makes this tensor fusion rather than bilinear fusion, and they are what buys the unimodal terms and the bias (Q20 of Exam 04). They also matter arithmetically: $129 \cdot 769$ is not $128 \cdot 768$.

The point of the question is the word “multiplicative”. Adding a modality does not add $d_3 \cdot h$ parameters, it multiplies the whole tensor by $(d_3+1)$. Going from two modalities to three took $5\times10^{7}$ weights — large but trainable — to $10^{11}$, which is more parameters than most language models and all of them in a single layer. There is no hardware answer to this; the operation simply does not scale past two modalities of any size.

Which is why the practical alternatives exist. FiLM gets multiplicative interaction for two parameters per channel. Cross-modal attention gets it for the cost of an attention layer, and scales to as many modalities as you can tokenise. Tensor fusion is worth knowing as the expressive upper bound and as the demonstration of why nobody uses it above two.
stem: Tensor fusion combines a $128$-dimensional text vector with a $768$-dimensional image vector into a hidden layer of width $512$. Give the number of weights. Then add a $2048$-dimensional video modality and give the new count and the factor.

explanation:
Answer: $\mathbf{500}$ and $\mathbf{2000}$ — quadratic in $\Delta\theta$, linear in $F$

\[\begin{aligned} \Omega_i(0.1) &= \tfrac12 \cdot 1000 \cdot 100 \cdot (0.1)^2 = \tfrac12 \cdot 1000 \cdot 100 \cdot 0.01 = 500 \\[2pt] \Omega_i(0.2) &= \tfrac12 \cdot 1000 \cdot 100 \cdot (0.2)^2 = \tfrac12 \cdot 1000 \cdot 100 \cdot 0.04 = 2000 \end{aligned}\] Doubling the movement quadrupled the penalty: quadratic in $\Delta\theta_i$, and plainly linear in $F_i$.

Why those two exponents are the design. $F_i$, the Fisher information, estimates how much the old task's loss depends on parameter $i$ — how much it would mind that parameter moving. Entering linearly, it acts as a per-parameter stiffness: important parameters are held firmly, unimportant ones are left free to be repurposed by the new task. That selectivity is the whole idea, and it is what distinguishes EWC from simply penalising all movement equally, which would prevent learning anything new.

The quadratic in $\Delta\theta$ makes the penalty a spring: negligible for small adjustments, sharply increasing for large ones. So a parameter can drift a little to accommodate the new task without being punished, and cannot be rewritten.

Where the whole approach still fails. EWC is a regularisation-based method, and it buys resistance to forgetting with plasticity. After enough tasks nearly every parameter has accumulated importance from something, the effective stiffness is high everywhere, and the model quietly stops being able to learn. That is the stability–plasticity dilemma arriving on schedule, and no choice of $\lambda$ escapes it.
stem: EWC penalises movement as $\Omega_i = \tfrac12\lambda F_i(\Delta\theta_i)^2$. With $\lambda = 1000$ and $F_i = 100$, give $\Omega_i$ for $\Delta\theta_i = 0.1$ and for $\Delta\theta_i = 0.2$, and state how the penalty scales in each of its two arguments.

explanation:
Answer: $\approx\mathbf{4.0\times10^{8}}$ evaluations; $\approx\mathbf{40}$ seconds a frame

\[\begin{aligned} \text{pixels} &= 1920 \cdot 1080 = 2{,}073{,}600 \\[2pt] \text{evaluations} &= 2{,}073{,}600 \cdot 192 = 398{,}131{,}200 \approx 3.98\times10^{8} \\[2pt] \text{time} &= 3.98\times10^{8} / 10^{7} \approx 39.8 \ \text{seconds} \end{aligned}\]

Nearly forty seconds for one frame, which matches the lecture's “up to a minute per frame” and is about $10^{3}$ times too slow for the $30$ fps that would make it interactive. Note that the model itself is small — a handful of megabytes of MLP. The cost is not the network's size but the number of times it is called, and that number is set by the rendering equation, not by the architecture.

Where the waste is. A ray through empty space still evaluates the network at every one of its samples, and every one returns $\sigma \approx 0$ and contributes exactly nothing to the integral. On a typical scene most samples are in empty space. Hierarchical sampling is the direct response: a coarse network first, build a pdf along the ray from the resulting weights $T_i\alpha_i$, and spend the fine network's samples where the weight actually is.

And this number is the argument for 3DGS. Its render step is rasterisation — project each Gaussian, sort by depth, blend — which is work a GPU does in fixed-function hardware. Not a faster network: no network. That is the one substitution, and interactive frame rates are its consequence.
stem: NeRF renders a $1920\times1080$ frame with $192$ samples per ray. Give the number of network evaluations for one frame, and the time it takes at $10^{7}$ evaluations per second.

explanation:
Marking points: the condition is overfitting. Three remedies with distinct mechanisms, for example: more or augmented data — the model must fit a larger, more varied sample, so memorising individual examples stops paying; weight decay — an explicit penalty on $\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert$ shrinks the hypothesis class towards smoother functions; dropout — units are removed at random during training, so no feature can rely on a fixed co-adaptation with another, which is equivalent to training an ensemble of sub-networks. Early stopping and reducing capacity are also acceptable.

The signature, precisely. Training loss falling while validation loss rises is overfitting. Both high and flat, with a small gap, is underfitting — a different condition needing the opposite treatment, and confusing them means adding regularisation to a model that already cannot fit its training set.

Why the marks are for the mechanisms. The three above act at genuinely different points: on the data, on the objective, and on the architecture during training. Listing three regularisers that all shrink weights is one idea written three ways.

Two details worth adding if there is room. Dropout is active in training and switched off at inference, with the activations rescaled so the expected value is unchanged — get that backwards and the network is silently mis-scaled at test time. And batch normalisation has an incidental regularising effect, because a sample's normalisation depends on the random batch it landed in, which is noise; removing BatchNorm can therefore cost accuracy for reasons that have nothing to do with conditioning.
stem: A model's training loss keeps falling while its validation loss rises. Name the condition, and give three distinct remedies together with the mechanism of each.

explanation:
Marking points: a CNN is given locality (each unit sees a small neighbourhood) and translation equivariance (the same kernel is applied at every position) by construction. A ViT is given neither: self-attention is global from the first layer and permutation equivariant, so it must learn from data that nearby patches are related and that a pattern means the same thing wherever it appears. That is why it needs far more data before it overtakes a comparable CNN.

Why an inductive bias is worth data. A convolution's weight sharing is a hard constraint saying that a cat in the corner is the same as a cat in the centre. A ViT can express that too, but it must discover it, and the only evidence available is examples of cats in various places. The constraint is free; the discovery is paid for in samples. This is the general trade: structure buys sample efficiency and costs generality.

And why the trade eventually flips. With enough data the learned version can be better than the imposed one, because it is not restricted to exactly translation equivariance and can find whatever regularity actually holds. This is the recurring pattern of the whole course — inductive biases are replaced by scale, and the engineering judgement is knowing which regime you are in. Concretely: use a CNN when training from scratch on limited data or deploying to an edge device.

What else follows from the same absence. No multi-scale hierarchy by construction either, which is why plain ViT is awkward as a detection backbone and why Swin's patch merging puts one back. The quadratic cost is a separate limitation, not a consequence of the missing bias.
stem: State what a plain ViT lacks that a CNN is given for free, and what it must therefore learn from data instead.

explanation:
Marking points: dense voxel grids are regular and simple but cost $O(r^3)$; hierarchical methods (OctNet, OGN) make empty space cheap, but still compute over it and give non-uniform feature resolution; sparse convolutions make it genuinely free by storing only active sites, but keep quantisation — and regular sparse convolution destroys the sparsity it depends on, which submanifold convolution fixes at the cost of disconnected components never communicating; point-based methods drop the grid and so lose quantisation error, but cannot represent free space and are usually less accurate; projection sidesteps 3D entirely to reuse 2D CNNs, and loses geometry, suffering distortion and occlusion.

Why the chain framing is the answer rather than a list. Each family is a response to a specific defect of the previous one, so the sequence is an argument. State the defect, not just the method.

Numbers that make the first step concrete. A chair occupies $10.41\%$ of a $32^3$ grid, $5.09\%$ of $64^3$, $2.41\%$ of $128^3$: as resolution rises you pay eight times more per doubling for a smaller fraction of useful voxels. And OctNet's founding observation is sharper than “3D is sparse” — activations concentrate near surfaces, so even a solid object's interior is waste.

The conclusion that must not be omitted. There is no winner. It is a task-dependent choice, and the reason 3D needs its own lecture at all is that — unlike images, which have a canonical pixel grid — 3D has no canonical representation. No free lunch, and the whole lecture is the enumeration of the menu.
stem: Each family of 3D method exists because of the previous one's failure. Trace that chain from dense voxel grids through to projection methods, naming the failure that motivates each step.

explanation:
Marking points: a per-node map must be equivariant — $f(PX, PAP^{\top}) = Pf(X,A)$ — so that relabelling the nodes relabels the outputs in the same way. A graph-level readout must be invariant — $f(PX, PAP^{\top}) = f(X,A)$ — so that the graph's single output does not depend on the order the nodes happened to be listed in. Swapping them breaks both: an invariant node map would give every node the same output, and an equivariant readout would give a graph-level prediction that changed when you renumbered the nodes.

Where the requirement comes from, which is worth stating first. There is exactly one assumption behind graph learning: a graph has no canonical node order. Everything else is derived. Since any ordering is as good as any other, a quantity describing the whole graph cannot depend on the choice, and a quantity attached to node $i$ must follow node $i$ wherever it is relabelled to.

The construction, and this is the part worth the marks. You get both at once by making the local aggregation invariant and sharing it across nodes. If $\mathbf{h}_i = g(\mathbf{x}_i, X_{\mathcal{N}_i})$ with $g$ invariant to the order of the neighbourhood, then the layer as a whole is automatically equivariant on the graph. Then one final invariant reduction — sum, mean or max over all nodes — turns the equivariant field into a graph-level answer. Note that “concatenate the neighbours' features” is not a valid aggregation, because concatenation depends on the order.

The concrete failure if they are swapped. Node classification with an invariant map would produce one label repeated $N$ times. Graph classification with an equivariant readout would produce a different molecule-toxicity prediction for the same molecule with its atoms listed in a different order — which is not a subtle bug but a model that is simply wrong.
stem: A GNN needs equivariance at one point and invariance at another. Say where each is required, and what would break if the two were swapped.

explanation:
Marking points: what is not new is the method — self-supervision, transformers and large-scale pre-training all predate the term. What is new is scale, and the consequence of scale: a single model that is adaptable to many tasks, including tasks nobody trained it for, through prompting or light adaptation rather than retraining.

The three properties, and why each is necessary rather than incidental. Massive broad data, because a model is foundational only where its data reached — the breadth of the training distribution is the breadth of the claim. Self-supervision, because nobody can label at that volume; it is the only available option, not a preference. High capacity, because a small model faced with everything averages it into mush; specialising to many domains at once requires somewhere to store the distinctions.

The good one-line framing. Machine learning stopped us hand-writing the algorithm; deep learning stopped us hand-writing the features; foundation models stop us hand-writing a model per application. Each step moved the human effort one level up.

And the honest qualification, which is what the question is really asking for. Nothing in the recipe would have surprised anyone in 2018. The surprise was empirical — that capability keeps arriving with scale, and that tasks outside the training objective become available at all. Answering “it is a new paradigm” without saying which part is old misses the question; so does “it is just a big model”, which misses that adaptability is a genuine change in how the thing is used.
stem: Explain in what sense a foundation model is something new, and in what sense it is not.

explanation:
Marking points: it establishes that the two feature distributions overlap — the classifier can no longer tell them apart. It does not establish that they overlap correctly, i.e. that source and target samples of the same class landed on top of each other. Alignment of the marginals says nothing about alignment of the class-conditionals, and the only evidence that matters is target-task performance.

The failure mode, concretely. Suppose the encoder maps target cars onto the region where source pedestrians live, and target pedestrians onto the source cars. The two clouds overlap perfectly, the domain classifier is at chance, the adversarial objective is fully satisfied — and the task head is now systematically wrong on every target sample. Nothing in the domain loss penalises this, because the domain loss cannot see the labels.

The reference value to quote. A fully confused two-class classifier has loss $2\ln 2 = 1.3863$ under the $50/50$ formulation. A value below that means the classifier is still winning and alignment is incomplete; reaching it means only that this particular diagnostic has stopped being informative.

What to do instead. Report target accuracy where any labels exist, even a small held-out set. Where none do, the honest position is that feature alignment is an assumption — it assumes a shared representation exists in which both domains can be expressed — and that its success cannot be verified from the domain classifier alone. This is the one real advantage of the rung below it on the ladder: importance weighting requires the source to cover the target, which is a strong assumption, but at least it is one you can check.
stem: After adversarial feature alignment a team reports that their domain classifier is down to $50\%$ accuracy, and concludes the adaptation worked. Say what that number does and does not establish.

explanation:
Marking points: (i) learnability — removing a little noise is a task a network can actually do, whereas mapping pure noise to a photograph in one step is the entire generative problem and no easier than the one you started with; (ii) Gaussianity — the reverse of a diffusion step is approximately Gaussian only when the step is small, and the whole parameterisation assumes it, since the model predicts a mean (and variance) of a Gaussian at each step.

The second reason is the technical one and is the one usually omitted. The forward step $q(\mathbf{x}_k\mid\mathbf{x}_{k-1}) = \mathcal{N}(\sqrt{1-\beta_k}\mathbf{x}_{k-1}, \beta_k I)$ is Gaussian by construction, but its reverse $q(\mathbf{x}_{k-1}\mid\mathbf{x}_k)$ is not — it involves the data distribution and is generally intractable. There is a classical result that it becomes Gaussian in the limit of small $\beta_k$. So the choice of many small steps is not merely convenient; it is what makes $p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{k-1}\mid\mathbf{x}_k) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\theta, \sigma_k^2 I)$ a well-founded model rather than a crude approximation. Take $K$ too small and the model is fitting a Gaussian to something that is not one, and no amount of training fixes it.

The first reason in one line. Each step is a denoiser, and denoising is a local, well-conditioned regression problem with a target we manufactured ourselves. Difficulty has been traded for repetition.

And note what it does not cost. Training is not $K$ times more expensive, because the closed form $\mathbf{x}_k = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}\mathbf{x}_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\varepsilon$ jumps straight to a randomly chosen level. The many steps are paid for only at sampling time — which is exactly the cost the ODE samplers later reclaimed.
stem: Why does DDPM chop the corruption into many small steps instead of learning to invert one large one? Give two distinct reasons.

explanation:
Marking points: an MLP taking raw coordinates is biased towards smooth functions — a spectral bias — so it cannot represent the high-frequency variation that surfaces, edges and texture consist of. Encoding each coordinate as $\gamma(p) = (\sin(2^k\pi p), \cos(2^k\pi p))_{k=0}^{K-1}$ supplies rapidly varying inputs, so a smooth function of those is a rapidly varying function of position. Without it the reconstruction comes out visibly blurred — recognisable geometry, no detail.

Why the bias exists at all. Two points close in input space have nearly identical activations at every layer of a coordinate MLP, so its output is nearly the same at both. That is a good prior for most regression problems and precisely the wrong one here, where the function being fitted is a scene: mostly flat, with the interesting content at the discontinuities.

Why sinusoids at rising frequencies specifically. Two positions a millimetre apart have almost identical values of $\sin(\pi p)$ but quite different values of $\sin(2^{9}\pi p)$. The encoding manufactures the separation the raw coordinate lacks, at a range of scales, so the network can be smooth in its own input space while being sharp in world space. The same trick, with the same justification, gives a transformer its positional encoding.

The comparison worth adding. 3DGS reaches high-frequency detail with no encoding at all, because it has no MLP and therefore no spectral bias — it simply places more, smaller Gaussians where detail is needed, via adaptive density control. Two solutions to one problem, and the difference follows from implicit against explicit.
stem: Explain why NeRF needs positional encoding, and what the result looks like without it.

explanation:
Any five-node graph with two components will do. Marks go to the matrices being consistent with the drawing and to the null space being identified correctly.

$\operatorname{rank}(L) = N - k = 5 - 2 = 3$, because the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $0$ equals the number of connected components, and the null space is spanned by their indicator vectors.

Why those vectors, in one line. $x^{\top}Lx = \sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}}(x_i-x_j)^2$, which is zero exactly when $x$ takes the same value at both ends of every edge — that is, when $x$ is constant on each component. Nothing else is in the kernel, and there are $k$ such vectors.

Two checks that catch almost every slip. The rows of $L$ sum to zero, so $L\mathbf{1} = 0$ always — a connected graph still has one zero eigenvalue. And $\operatorname{trace}(L) = \sum_i\deg(i) = 2|\mathcal{E}| = 6$ here, which must also equal the sum of the eigenvalues; with three of them zero, the remaining two must sum to $6$.
stem: Draw a graph of five nodes forming two connected components. Beside it write its adjacency matrix $A$ and its unnormalised Laplacian $L = D - A$, and mark the vectors spanning the null space of $L$. Then state in one sentence what $\operatorname{rank}(L)$ is and why.

explanation:
The three regions and the collapse line are the marks. The horizontal line is what the question is really about.

$\mathcal{L} = \max\{0,\ \mathcal{D}_p - \mathcal{D}_n + m\}$: a straight line of slope $-1$, hitting zero at $\mathcal{D}_n = \mathcal{D}_p + m$ and flat thereafter. The three regions fall out of it — easy beyond $\mathcal{D}_p+m$ with zero loss and therefore zero gradient; semi-hard between $\mathcal{D}_p$ and $\mathcal{D}_p+m$ with $0 < \mathcal{L} < m$; hard below $\mathcal{D}_p$ with $\mathcal{L} \ge m$ always.

The two sentences asked for. A constant embedding makes every distance zero, so it pays exactly $\mathcal{L} = m$ on every triplet — the green line — and that is the price the optimiser is comparing everything against. Every hard negative sits in the shaded region above that line, so a diet of hard negatives makes collapse the cheaper option and the network takes it; semi-hard negatives are the ones strictly between $0$ and $m$, which is why they are the useful ones: expensive enough to produce a gradient, cheap enough that collapsing would make matters worse.

What the picture also shows. Raising $m$ raises the green line and the whole sloped segment together, so it does not remove the collapse solution — it moves both sides of the comparison. And the easy region is genuinely flat, not merely small: those triplets are not weakly informative, they are exactly zero, which is why they are called invalid rather than easy in some treatments.
stem: Plot the triplet loss as a function of $\mathcal{D}_n$, for a fixed $\mathcal{D}_p$ and margin $m$. Mark the easy, semi-hard and hard regions on the axis, and mark the loss a fully collapsed network pays. Then explain in two sentences why that last value is the one that matters.

explanation:
Both directions on one diagram, with the fixed one and the learned one clearly distinguished, and the closed-form shortcut drawn as the jump it is.

The one sentence asked for. The reverse of a diffusion step is Gaussian only in the limit of a small step: $q(\mathbf{x}_{k-1}\mid\mathbf{x}_k)$ involves the data distribution and is intractable in general, but as $\beta_k \to 0$ it tends to a Gaussian, which is what licenses modelling it as $\mathcal{N}(\mu_\theta, \sigma_k^2 I)$ at all.

What each label on the diagram is doing. The forward chain has no parameters — it is a fixed corruption schedule we chose, which is why nothing is learned along the top. The network's output is the noise $\varepsilon_\theta$, and the mean follows from it, \[ \mu_\theta(\mathbf{x}_k,k) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_k}} \left(\mathbf{x}_k - \frac{1-\alpha_k}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}}\, \varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf{x}_k,k)\right), \] so predicting noise and predicting the reverse mean are the same model in different clothes. The amber jump is what makes training affordable: a random $k$ is chosen per example and $\mathbf{x}_k$ is produced in one operation, never by running the chain.

Worth marking if you have room. The score and the noise prediction differ by a known constant, $s_\theta = -\varepsilon_\theta/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}$ — which is the line that identifies DDPM with score matching, and hence with everything in the SDE picture.
stem: Draw the DDPM forward and reverse chains as one diagram from $\mathbf{x}_0$ to $\mathbf{x}_K$. Label which direction is fixed and which is learned, what the network outputs, and where the closed-form shortcut applies. Then state in one sentence what makes the reverse step approximately Gaussian.

explanation:
initialise $\theta_k \leftarrow \theta_q$; queue $\leftarrow$ empty ring buffer of $K$ keys\ for each batch $x$:\ *1.5em$x^q, x^k \leftarrow \mathrm{aug}(x), \mathrm{aug}(x)$ two views of the same images\ *1.5em$q \leftarrow f_{\theta_q}(x^q)$\ *1.5em$k^{+} \leftarrow f_{\theta_k}(x^k)$, detached no gradient on the key branch\ *1.5em$\ell^{+} \leftarrow q\cdot k^{+}/\tau$; $\ell^{-}_j \leftarrow q\cdot \text{queue}[j]/\tau$ for all $j$\ *1.5em$\mathcal{L} \leftarrow \mathrm{CrossEntropy} \bigl([\ell^{+}, \ell^{-}_1,\dots,\ell^{-}_{K}],\ \text{label}=0\bigr)$ InfoNCE, a $(K{+}1)$-way choice\ *1.5emupdate $\theta_q$ by gradient descent on $\mathcal{L}$\ *1.5em$\theta_k \leftarrow m\,\theta_k + (1-m)\,\theta_q$ momentum, $m \approx 0.999$\ *1.5emenqueue $k^{+}$; dequeue the oldest FIFO

Why the key encoder is not updated by gradient descent. The queue holds keys computed at many different past steps, and they all compete as answers to the same question, so they have to remain mutually comparable. A gradient-updated key encoder would move as fast as the query encoder and a key from a thousand steps ago would effectively have come from a different network; the momentum update makes it drift slowly enough that the whole queue stays coherent.

What the queue buys over a larger batch. It decouples the number of negatives from the batch size. The InfoNCE bound is $MI \ge \log N - \mathcal{L}$, so more negatives is a higher ceiling — but computing the exact gradient over $N$ in-batch negatives means keeping all $N$ sets of activations in the backward graph, which is why SimCLR needs $B = 8192$. The queue stores only the feature vectors, with no gradient: $65{,}536 \times 128 \times 4$ bytes is about $32$ MB, and MoCo v2 matches SimCLR at a batch of $256$.

Two details easy to leave out. The two augmentations are of the same images, which is what makes $k^{+}$ a positive at all. And the label passed to the cross-entropy is always index $0$, because the positive is placed first — the loss is quite literally an $(K{+}1)$-way classification whose correct answer is known by construction.

And the limitation the design does not fix. Negatives are drawn without regard to class, so two images of different dogs become a false negative and the loss actively pushes them apart. Bigger datasets make this worse, not better, and it is one of the reasons the field moved on to self-distillation, which needs no negatives at all — and inherited collapse instead.
stem: Write pseudo-code for MoCo: the query encoder, the momentum key encoder, the queue, and the InfoNCE loss. Then state in one sentence why the key encoder is not updated by gradient descent, and in one sentence what the queue buys over simply using a larger batch.
